title: Bill of indictment for fraud: Joseph Johnson late of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Joseph Johnson late of the House of Correction at Northallerton labourer for obtaining five guineas from Robert Kirby by falsely pretending to Robert Kirby that he was agent for Thomas Wilson of 24 Lincoln's Inn Field's, London, and produced a letter signed by Wilson to the effect that he should be advanced up to £20 in money from the account of Thomas Wilson should it be needed during his stay in Stockton.  Johnson also pretended to Kirby, who was cashier and principal clerk in the Malton and Whitby Bank at Whitby, that he had purchased a ship called the Minerva lying in Whitby harbour on Wilson's behalf, producing a promissory note for five guineas and requesting an advance of the same amount. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 27 October 1813. Endorsed with name of witness and "a true bill found"

Bradley had falsely pretended to Jane Ross wife of Thomas Ross that he was from the ship "James" which was in Whitby harbour laden with ironstone Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 25 April 1850. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Fanny Walker or Frances Walker or Finlay of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Fanny Walker otherwise called Frances Walker otherwise called Frances Finlay late of the House of Correction at Northallerton labourer for stealing one cotton quilt value 3s and one blanket value 3s, the property of Brown Marshall. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 5 September 1850. Walker/Finlay had previously been convicted of felony at the Quarter Sessions for county Durham held at Durham on 2 July 1849. Endorsed with names of witnesses and " a true bill"With certificate of conviction at the Quarter Sessions for county Durham held at Durham on 2 July 1849 of Frances Finlay wife of Thomas Finlay late of the parish of Jarrow in county Durham labourer for stealing two flannel petticoats value 1s and one pair of flannel drawers value 1s, the property of Sarah Dickinson at the parish of Jarrow on 7 June 1849.  Finlay was sentenced to hard labour in the House of Correction at Durham for two calendar months.  Certificate dated 11 October 1850

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Henry Dickinson of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Henry Dickinson late of the House of Correction at Northallerton labourer for stealing 16 hams value £8 and 25 stones weight of ham value £8, the property of Robert Sawdon. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 3 May 1851. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Evan Clayton or Cleeton of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Evan Clayton otherwise called Evan Cleeton late of the House of Correction at Northallerton labourer for stealing one pair of boots value 5s, the property of James Elder. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 4 October 1850. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Margaret Garrett of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Margaret Garrett late of the House of Correction at Northallerton wife of Andrew Garrett of Whitby labourer for stealing ten yards of merino cloth value 10s, the property of James Nicholson Clarkson. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 18 October 1850. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Henry Dickinson of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Henry Dickinson late of the House of Correction at Northallerton labourer for stealing six hams value £3 and seven stones weight of ham value £3, the property of Robert Sawdon. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 14 March 1851. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for assault: Gideon Smales of Whitby
description: Bill of indictment of Gideon Smales late of the township of Whitby timber merchant for assaulting William Fortune Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 28 November 1820. Endorsed with name of witness and "no bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Charles Wright
description: Bill of indictment of Charles Wright stealing money, and one silver watch, one German silver watchguard, and one purse, value together £5 and more, the property of Peter Thomas Mauger and taken from his dwelling house. Offence committed at Whitby on 16 December 1856. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: David Harris
description: Bill of indictment of David Harris for stealing £11 10s in money, the property of John Flanders, from the ship called the "Cupid" in Whitby Harbour. Offence committed at Whitby on 23 June 1857. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Midsummer Quarter Sessions: records relating to attendance at the Sessions
description: This sub-series contains records relating to attendance at the Sessions, and includes:- call roll, including a precept (dated 4 June 1851) to the sheriff to appear at the Quarter Sessions and to summon jurors and justices to the Sessions to be held at Northallerton on 1 July 1851.  Includes names of those on Grand and Traverse Juries, and names of the sheriff, deputy sheriff, treasurer, coroners, high constables, bailiffs and keepers of the gaol at the castle of York and of the House of Correction at Northallerton [1 item]- apologies for absence from the Sessions of Robert Raine Henderson sheriff's officer [1 item]- papers relating to exemption from jury service of Isaac Parker, Thomas Barry, James Dobson and Robert Hugginson [5 items]- warrants to the bailiffs of Gilling West, Langbaurgh East and Whitby Strand to summon jurors for the Grand Jury and Traverse Jury [3 items]

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: William George Taylor
description: Bill of indictment of William George Taylor for stealing two jet bracelets, 26 pieces of jet, one other piece of jet, and seven pounds weight of jet, the property of William Wright. Includes indictment of Taylor for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed at the parish of Whitby on 11 August 1855. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "no bill"

title: Easter Quarter Sessions 1839: records relating to appointments
description: This sub-series contains records relating to appointments, and includes:- notice of appointment of a returning officer for Whitby [1 item]

title: Bill of indictment: Margaret Garrett
description: Bill of indictment of Margaret Garrett for stealing ten pounds weight of beef, the property of John Wilkinson and Joseph Wilkinson. Offence committed on 24 December 1852. Garrett had previously been convicted of felony at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 31 December 1850. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 31 December 1850 of Margaret Garrett late of the House of Correction at Northallerton wife of Andrew Garrett of Whitby labourer for stealing 40 yards of cotton print, the property of Matthew Thistle and Thomas Pressick Yeoman at the township of Whitby.  Garrett was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for six calendar months.  Certificate dated 1 January 1853

title: Bill of indictment: Robert Gaines
description: Bill of indictment of Robert Gaines for obtaining four pounds weight of bacon from Thomas Franks by falsely pretending to him that he (Gaines) had been sent for the bacon by Mary Robinson of Kelly's Yard in Whitby lodging house keeper (meaning Mary wife of John Robertson [sic] of Kelly's Yard lodging house keeper, who was known as Mary Robinson) who was known to Franks in his business as a provision dealer Offence committed on 5 February 1858. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for obtaining money under false pretences; George Turner the younger
description: Bill of indictment of George Turner the younger for obtaining money by falsely pretending to Elizabeth Fletcher that he had been to the farm and seen her husband George Fletcher who said she was to give Turner 3s as he had nothing in his pocket but a sovereign and a shilling. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 10 April 1856. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Christmas Quarter Sessions: coroners' records
description: This sub-series contains coroner's records, and includes:- abstract of inquisitions and expenses of the coroner for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand [1 bundle]

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Thomas Lloyd
description: Bill of indictment of Thomas Lloyd for stealing one pair of boots, the property of James Hunter, from the vessel called the "Unity" in Whitby Harbour. Offence committed at Whitby on 15 November 1856. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment: Robert Gaines
description: Bill of indictment of Robert Gaines for obtaining three pounds weight of bacon and seven eggs from Peter Appleton by falsely pretending to him that he (Gaines) had been sent for the bacon and three-pennyworth of eggs by Ann Robinson of Church Street in Whitby toy dealer who was known to Franks in his business as a provision dealer Offence committed on 19 February 1858. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Midsummer Quarter Sessions: records relating to attendance at the Sessions
description: This sub-series contains records relating to attendance at the Sessions, and includes:- call roll, including a precept (dated 26 May 1858) to the sheriff to appear at the Quarter Sessions and to summon jurors and justices to the Sessions to be held at Northallerton on 29 June 1858.  With names of those on Grand and Traverse Juries, and names of the sheriff, deputy sheriff, treasurer, coroners, high constables, bailiffs and keepers of the gaol at the castle of York and of the House of Correction at Northallerton [1 item]- papers relating to the exemption from jury service of Mr Waddington, Hugh Kenwood Davey, William Nicholson, John Gibson, Thomas Rowland, Joseph Campion, Captain Elevon and Mr Kirby [12 items]- warrants to the bailiffs of Hang West, Langbaurgh East and Whitby Strand to summon jurors for the Grand Jury and Traverse Jury [3 items]- list of members of a jury [1 item]- apology of Thomas Masterman for absence at the Sessions [1 item]

title: Bill of indictment: Robert Veneson of Newholm cum Dunsley
description: Bill of indictment of Robert Veneson late of Newholm cum Dunsley farmer and a packer of butter for sale for selling ten firkins of butter that were each deficient in weight by four pounds value 4d per pound from the true weight of 56 pounds. Offence committed at Whitby on 4 August 1694. Endorsed with name of witness and "true bill"With presentment at Quarter Sessions at Stokesley on 14 August 1694

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Solomon Marshall
description: Bill of indictment of Solomon Marshall for stealing 42 jet beads, the property of George Shevill. Offence committed on 8 November 1872. Marshall had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 26 October 1869. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Benjamin Shaw
description: Bill of indictment of Benjamin Shaw for stealing one chain and two keys, the property of John O'Hara. Offence committed on 21 February 1872. Shaw had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 8 November 1870. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 8 November 1870 of Benjamin Shaw for stealing £6 10s in money, the property of William Thirlwall.  Shaw was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for two calendar months.  Certificate dated 1 April 1872

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Bridget Hirst or Douglass
description: Bill of indictment of Bridget Hirst otherwise Bridget Douglass for stealing £2 6s in money, the property of Joseph Smith and taken from his person. Offence committed on 12 October 1869. Hirst/Douglass had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 4 February 1865. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill found"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 4 February 1865 of Bridget Douglass for stealing 35s in money and one jet brooch, the property of Thomas Anderson and stolen from his person.  Douglass was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for two calendar months.  Certificate dated 18 October 1869

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Farthing
description: Bill of indictment of William Farthing for stealing three pounds weight of beef, the property of Richard Rooke. Offence committed on 10 February 1872. Farthing had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 11 January 1870. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 11 January 1870 of William Farthing for stealing four pounds weight of beef, the property of John Beal.  Farthing was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for two calendar months.  Certificate dated 1 April 1872

title: Michaelmas Quarter Sessions: records returned into Quarter Sessions
description: This sub-series contains records returned into Quarter Sessions, and includes:- alehouse recognizances: Birdforth; Bulmer; Gilling East; Gilling West; Langbaurgh East; Pickering Lythe West; and Whitby Strand [8 items]

title: Recognizances in the case against Mary King of Whitby
description: Recognizance made by Henry Gibson of the township of Whitby police constable for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to prefer a bill of indictment against Mary King of the township of Whitby for stealing two shirts, the property of Robert Day. Recognizance made by Charles Tempest Clarkson of the township of Whitby superintendent of police for the appearance of Sarah Day wife of Robert Day of the township of Whitby jet worker at the next Quarter Sessions to give evidence in the case against Mary King

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Solomon Marshall
description: Bill of indictment of Solomon Marshall for stealing six pounds weight of jet, the property of Richard Thompson. Offence committed on 11 November 1872. Marshall had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 26 October 1869. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 26 October 1869 of Solomon Marshall for stealing three jet hearts, three jet top pieces, three jet bottom pieces, four jet shackles and four banjo screws, the property of Samuel Trueman.  Marshall was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for three calendar months.  Certificate dated 24 December 1872

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: Mary Murphy
description: Bill of indictment of Mary Murphy for stealing 71/2d in money, the property of John Wright. Includes indictment of Murphy for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed on 15 September 1873. Murphy had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 8 March 1873. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 8 March 1873 of Mary Murphy for stealing four rabbit skins, the property of John Wright.  Murphy was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for three calendar months.  Certificate dated 10 October 1873

title: Bill of indictment for misdemeanour: John Woodward, Thomas Busby, Robert Hogg, James Crayford and Thomas Taylor
description: Bill of indictment of John Woodward, Thomas Busby, Robert Hogg, James Crayford and Thomas Taylor on two counts of placing a railway trolley or bogy on the Stockton and Whitby branch of the North Eastern Railway in the parish of Guisborough and propelling it along the line. Offence committed on 3 August 1873. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Thomas Gay
description: Bill of indictment of Thomas Gay servant to William Lewis for embezzling 10s from his employer. Offence committed on 1 May 1880. Gay had previously been convicted of felony at Whitby Petty Sessions on 12 November 1867. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at Whitby on 12 November 1867 of William Ripley and Thomas Gay for stealing one bottle of currant whisky, eight ounces of powder, one box of gun caps and one pamphlet value 5s, the property of Roger Dobson, at the township of Ruswarp on 1 November 1867.  Ripley and Gay were sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for one calendar month.  Certificate dated 23 June 1880

title: Bill of indictment: George Burns
description: Bill of indictment of George Burns servant to John Porritt for embezzling £3, the property of his master. Offence committed on 28 July 1877. Burns had previously been convicted of felony at the Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 24 March 1877. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill" With certificate of conviction at the Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 24 March 1877 of George Burns for stealing a wagon shoe value 12s, the property of James Atkinson and Henry Beeforth, at the township of Glaisdale on 23 March 1877.  Burns was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for 21 days.  Certificate dated 15 October 1878

title: Bill of indictment: Harriet Ann Suggitt
description: Bill of indictment of Harriet Ann Suggitt for obtaining one pound of cheese and a loaf of bread from Henry Wald grocer by falsely pretending to him that she was servant to Charles Beyerbach of Whitby and that she had been sent by Beyerbach for half a pound of tea, two stones of flour, a quarter of a stone of lump sugar, half a pound of corn flour, two ounces of baking powder, one pound of currants, one pound of sultans raisins, one pound of cheese, a loaf of bread and one pound of moist sugar. Offence committed on 18 May 1882. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "no bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Foxton
description: Bill of indictment of William Foxton for plundering a vessel called the "J.H. Lorentzen" then stranded on shore and stealing one piece of metal value 1s 6d, the property of Thomas Jones. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 21 March 1879. Foxton had previously been convicted of felony at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 2 January 1877. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 2 January 1877 of William Foxton for stealing two hind legs of a sheep, at the township of Redmire on 29 October 1876.  Foxton was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for nine calendar months.  Certificate dated 30 March 1881

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: William Russell
description: Bill of indictment of William Russell for stealing one pair of men's boots, the property of William Johnson. Includes indictment of Russell for receiving the said goods. Offences committed on 1 December 1877. Russell had previously been convicted of felony at the Petty Sessions at Whitby on 21 April 1877. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill. With certificate of conviction before three Justices at Whitby on 21 April 1877 of William Russell for stealing one top coat and one sealskin cap valued together at £1 0s 6d, the property of George Reeves, at the township of Mickleby on 15 April 1877.  Russell was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for two calendar months, to begin at the end of another term of imprisonment to which Russell had been sentenced.  Certificate dated 19 December 1877

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: Janet Ventress otherwise Jane Ventriss
description: Bill of indictment of Janet Ventress otherwise called Jane Ventriss for stealing one sheet, the property of Mary Stubbs. Includes indictment of Ventress/Ventriss for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed on 9 April 1880. Ventress/Ventriss had previously been convicted of felony at Whitby Petty Sessions on 17 February 1880. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at the Whitby Strand Petty Sessions held on 17 February 1880 of Jane Ventriss wife of George Ventriss of the township of Whitby gardener for stealing one chemise value 1s, the property of Ann Bedlington, at the township of Whitby on 31 January 1880.  Ventriss was sentenced to hard labour at the prison at Northallerton for 14 days.  Certificate dated 23 June 1880

title: Midsummer Quarter Sessions: records relating to oaths of office
description: This sub-series contains records relating to oaths of office, and includes:- oaths of the returning officers of the boroughs of Malton, Northallerton and Whitby [3 items]

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: Jane Ventress or Ventriss
description: Bill of indictment of Jane Ventress otherwise called Jane Ventriss for stealing one sheet and a flannel vest, the property of George Lorrains. Includes indictment of Ventress/Ventriss for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed on 24 August 1881. Ventress/Ventriss had previously been convicted of felony at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 29 June 1880. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 29 June 1880 of Ventress/Ventriss for stealing one sheet, the property of Mary Stubbs, at the township of Whitby on 9 April 1880.  Ventress/Ventriss, with a previous conviction for felony, was sentenced to hard labour at the prison at Northallerton for two calendar months.  Certificate dated 15 October 1881

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: Hannah Thompson
description: Bill of indictment of Hannah Thompson for stealing one crumb cloth, the property of Thomas Harland. Includes indictment of Thompson for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed on 1 November 1881. Thompson, formerly Hannah Marsay, had previously been convicted of felony at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 5 January 1864. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 5 January 1864 of Hannah Marsay for stealing one pair of boots and one shawl, the property of Hannah Wilson, at the township of Whitby on 21 November 1863.  Marsay was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for one calendar month and then was to be sent to a reformatory and industrial school for five years.  Certificate dated 2 January 1882

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: George Jackson
description: Bill of indictment of George Jackson for stealing one spade, the property of Laverick Robinson. Includes indictment of Jackson for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed on 8 October 1886. Jackson had previously been convicted of felony at Petty Sessions at Whitby held on 23 August 1873. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at Whitby Petty Sessions on 23 August 1873 of George Jackson and Thomas Brown for stealing 40 pots value 10s, the property of Elizabeth Darnton on 21 August 1873 at the township of Lythe.  Jackson and Brown were sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for one calendar month.  Certificate dated 16 October 1886

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Dalton of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of William Dalton late of the House of Correction at Northallerton labourer for stealing 400 pounds weight of bones value 10s, the property of George Chapman and Jonathan Featherstone. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 13 January 1837. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Catherine MacNuff or Fawcett or Dogherty or Maxfield of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Catherine MacNuff otherwise called Catherine Fawcett otherwise called Catherine Dogherty otherwise called Catherine Maxfield late of the House of Correction at Northallerton singlewoman for stealing five hare skins value 1s and eight rabbit skins value 1s, the property of Thomas Gilroy. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 12 January 1838. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for nuisance: the inhabitants of Ugglebarnby
description: Bill of indictment of the inhabitants of the township of Ugglebarnby for not repairing part of the king's highway from Sneaton to Pickering. From 1 January 1814 the highway has been in disrepair in the township of Ugglebarnby in the parish of Whitby from Sneaton Boundary Stone on the west side of the highway near Falling Foss Cottage north-eastward towards the town of Sneaton, being 429 feet in length and 30 feet in breadth. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for misdemeanour: Patrick Connelly
description: Bill of indictment of Patrick Connelly for assaulting Robert Coulson. Offences committed at the parish of Whitby on 23 June 1883. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: Margaret Eliza Gazzard otherwise Eliza Gazzard
description: Bill of indictment of Margaret Eliza Gazzard otherwise called Eliza Gazzard for stealing four counterpanes, two pairs of blankets, one book, one pair of sheets, and one table cloth, the property of Charles Styles. Includes indictment of Gazzard for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed on 8 September 1877. Gazzard had previously been convicted of felony at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 16 October 1866. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 16 October 1866 of Eliza Gazzard for stealing two blankets, three sheets, two shirts, one pair of boots, one towel, two pillows, and one bolster, the property of John Kay, at the township of Whitby on 5 September 1865.  Gazzard was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for six weeks.  Certificate dated 17 October 1877

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Garbutt
description: Bill of indictment of William Garbutt for breaking into the dwelling house of Thomas Ruddock at Castleton in the parish of Danby with intent to steal. Offence committed on 13 April 1873. Garbutt had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 26 November 1872. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 26 November 1872 of William Garbutt for stealing £11 in money and five pounds weight of jet, the property of George Locker.  Garbutt was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for four calendar months.  Certificate dated 24 June 1873

title: Bill of indictment for felony: John Davis
description: Bill of indictment of John Davis for stealing one hat, one waistcoat and one pair of trousers, the property of Edward Theaker Weatherill. Offence committed on 29 June 1873. David had previously been convicted at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 2 August 1870. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 2 August 1870 of John Davis for stealing one shirt, the property of Henry Ward.  Davis was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for two calendar months.  Certificate dated 2 July 1873

title: Bill of indictment for felony and receiving stolen goods: Ann Marshall, Robert Wilson and Fanny Wilson, all of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Ann Marshall late of the House of Correction at Northallerton singlewoman for stealing five pieces of copper bolts value 2d, two pairs of trousers value 1s, one pair of bellows value 1s, two flat smoothing irons value 1s, two hats value 2s, three knives value 1s, three forks value 1s, one brass candlestick value 6d, one Italian iron value 6d, one fire shovel value 6d, one holland slip value 6d, two yards of calico value 2d, and two aprons value 2d, the property of George Lockey. Includes indictment of Robert Wilson labourer and Fanny his wife, both late of the House of Correction at Northallerton, for receiving two pairs of trousers value 1s, one pair of bellows value 1s, two flat smoothing irons value 1s, two hats value 2s, three knives value 1s, three forks value 1s, one brass candlestick value 6d, one Italian iron value 6d, one fire shovel value 6d, one holland slip value 6d, two yards of calico value 2d, and two aprons value 2d knowing them to be stolen. Offences committed at the parish of Whitby on 23 June 1836. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Elizabeth Constable
description: Bill of indictment of Elizabeth Constable for stealing two pillow cases and four sheets, the property of Thomas Ward. Offence committed on 13 December 1873. Constable had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 22 January 1870. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 22 January 1870 of Elizabeth Constable for stealing a quantity of chips and of scrap iron, the property of Thomas Turnbull.  Constable was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for seven days. Certificate dated 30 June 1874

title: Bill of indictment for felony: John Shipman
description: Bill of indictment of John Shipman for breaking into the shop of William Douthwaite in the parish of Whitby and stealing five stones weight of flour and one sack, the property of the said William Douthwaite. Offence committed on 22 January 1875. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Johnson
description: Bill of indictment of William Johnson for stealing 10s in money, the property of William Gill the younger. Offence committed on 1 February 1875. Johnson had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 23 November 1869. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 23 November 1869 of William Johnson for stealing one pair of clogs, the property of Henry Thompson.  Johnson was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for 42 days and then was to be sent to a reformatory school for four years.  Certificate dated 19 February 1875

title: Bill of indictment for misdemeanour: Anne Elizabeth Patton
description: Bill of indictment of Anne Elizabeth Patton for obtaining one polonaise and one black satin skirt from Henry Duck by falsely pretending that Mistress Coward was the upper housemaid at the Royal Hotel in Whitby and had lived there for the preceding two summers, and had sent Patton for some ready-made dresses for her (Coward's) inspection. Patton had taken two polonaises and then claimed that Mistress Coward had approved of one of them. Offence committed on 9 October 1875. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With draft indictment of Ann Elizabeth Patton

Some names on the jury lists are annotated with ticks, circles, and "s" [possibly for "sworn"], but these annotations are not included in the list below.  The names of the bailiffs are also given in the jury lists, but again, these have not been included below. Call roll. Sir William Ingilby baronet, sheriff of the county of York. Thomas Paul gentleman, his deputy for the North Riding. Valentine Kitchingman esquire, Treasurer for the North Riding. Coroners- Thomas Harrison of Kirby Moorside- George Brigham of Rudby- William Dinsdale of Aiskew- Henry Belcher of Whitby- Samuel Cowling of York. High Constables- James Langdale and Christopher Hudson gentlemen for Allertonshire- James Barker and Thomas Scott gentlemen for Birdforth- William Ware and John Plowman gentlemen for Bulmer- George Readman and Thomas Meek gentlemen for Gilling East- Thomas Lax and Samuel Spedding gentlemen for Gilling West- John Plews and George Dryden gentlemen for Hang East- Thomas Place and Ralph Lodge gentlemen for Hang West- William Fall and Tristram Walker gentlemen for Hallikeld- George Brigham and Joseph Hickson gentlemen for Langbaurgh- Peter Marshall and Thomas Bointon gentlemen for Pickering Lythe- George Carter and John Reed gentlemen for Ryedale- Thomas Galilee Dale gentleman for Whitby Strand. Bailiffs- Thomas Flower for Allertonshire- Robert Armitage for Birdforth- James Monkman for Bulmer- William Fall for Gilling East and Gilling West- William Slater the younger for Hang East and Hallikeld- Leonard Holmes for Hang West- John Watson for Langbaurgh- Jerom Nares for Pickering Lythe- Richard Trenam for Ryedale- Thomas Horsman for Whitby Strand. William Staveley keeper of the Gaol at the Castle of York. Thomas Shepherd keeper of the House of Correction at Northallerton. Precept, call roll and lists of jurors are all joined together

title: Bill of indictment for not repairing the king's highway: the inhabitants of the township of Hawsker cum Stainsacre
description: Bill of indictment of the inhabitants of the township of Hawsker cum Stainsacre for not repairing part of the highway from Low Hawsker to Whitby. From 3 January 1823 the highway has been in disrepair in the township of Hawsker cum Stainsacre from the south end of the hamlet of Low Hawsker northward towards the town of Whitby, being 300 yards in length and 6 yards in breadth. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "bill found"With copy

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Joseph Hugill of Whitby
description: Bill of indictment of Joseph Hugill late of the parish of Whitby labourer for plundering one guard board value 1d, ten planks measuring 10 feet long by 1 foot broad value 1d each, 10 feet of wood value 1d, one hundredweight of wood value 1d, and one hundredweight of timber value 1d, belonging to a ship called the "Acorn", the property of Joseph Haycock, stranded and cast on shore at the parish of Whitby. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 16 January 1823. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for not repairing the king's highway: the inhabitants of Moorsholm
description: Bill of indictment of the inhabitants of the township of Moorsholm for not repairing part of the highway from Guisborough to Kirby Moorside. From 7 July 1821 the highway has been in disrepair in the township of Moorsholm from a stone on the highway from Guisborough to Whitby westward towards Kirby Moorside to another stone near a hill called Todhow, being 2,531 yards in length and 13 feet in breadth; and also from a stone on the highway marked with the letter "D" westward to Kirby Moorside to another stone marked Danby Road, being 731 yards in length and 13 feet in breadth. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Midsummer Quarter Sessions: records relating to attendance at the Sessions
description: This sub-series contains records relating to attendance at the Sessions, and includes:- call roll, including a precept (dated 25 June 1823) to the sheriff to appear at the Quarter Sessions and to summon jurors and justices to the Sessions to be held at Northallerton on 28 July 1823. title: Presentment for nuisance in not repairing a bridge: the inhabitants of the North Riding
description: Presentment of the inhabitants of the North Riding for not maintaining New Bridge over the river Esk on the highway between Glaisdale and Whitby in the parishes of Danby and Egton. From 9 January 1823 the bridge, being 60 feet in length and 10 feet in breadth, has been in disrepair. With a statement from George Atkinson and Matthew Peacock saying that the bridge was accustomed to be repaired by the inhabitants of Glaisdale and Egton, and requesting that the inhabitants of the North Riding should be discharged

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Cock, Marshall Salton and William Nendick all of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of William Cock carpenter, Marshall Salton carpenter and William Nendick mariner, all late of the House of Correction at Northallerton, for stealing one anchor value 3d, one iron cadge value 3d, and two hundredweight of iron value 3d, belonging to a stranded ship called the "Outhwaite", the property of Richard Greenwell and John Hope. Offences committed at the parish of Whitby on 8 or 9 September 1824. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Certificate of indisposition: John Calvert
description: Certificate of John Earnshaw surgeon and apothecary at Whitby that John Calvert bailiff cannot attend the Sessions because of a complaint in his side and bladder which has afflicted him since July

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Ann Cook of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Bill of indictment of Ann Cook late of the House of Correction at Northallerton widow for stealing 15 pounds weight of cheese value 10d, the property of John Anderson. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 16 October 1824. Endorsed with names of witnesses and annotated "a true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Ward
description: Bill of indictment of William Ward for stealing one pewter wash basin, one mortar, one pestle, and eight pounds weight of lead, the property of Appleton Stephenson; and 16 pounds weight of lead, the property of the churchwardens of the parish of Whitby. Offence committed on 13 April 1854. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: James Nugent and Catherine Nugent
description: Bill of indictment of James Nugent for stealing one jacket, one handkerchief, one pair of trousers, two flannel shirts, two pairs of braces, one neckerchief, three pairs of stockings, one frock, one shirt, one pair of mittens, two comforters, and two smocks, the property of John Smith. Includes indictment of Catherine Nugent for receiving the stolen goods Offences committed on 7 January 1860. James Nugent had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 28 November 1857. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 28 November 1857 of James Nugent for stealing two stones weight of rags, the property of Henry Miller.  Nugent was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for 42 days.  Certificate dated 29 March 1860

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Thomas Parker
description: Bill of indictment of Thomas Parker for stealing 21 pounds weight of hay, the property of Ann Addison. Offence committed on 2 February 1860. Parker had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 21 May 1859. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 21 May 1859 of Thomas Parker for stealing one pair of wellington boots, the property of John Norman.  Parker was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for three calendar months.  Certificate dated 29 March 1860

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Robinson Keld
description: Bill of indictment of Robinson Keld for stealing 4s 71/2d in money and one till, the property of Vallance Cole Offence committed on 1 February 1860. Keld had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 26 January 1858. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 26 January 1858 of Robinson Keld the younger for stealing one gold bracelet, the property of Francis Ayre Raw and taken from his dwelling house.  Keld was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for three calendar months.  Certificate dated 29 March 1860

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Owen Mahon
description: Bill of indictment of Owen Mahon for stealing one silver watch, one silver watch chain, one gold watch key and one brass watch key value £5 and more, the property of Andrew Turner and taken from his dwelling house in the township of Whitby. Offence committed on 25 August 1860. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Rebecca Tweedie
description: Bill of indictment of Rebecca Tweedie for stealing seven pounds weight of bacon, the property of William Piercy. Offence committed on 19 February 1870. Tweedie had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 18 December 1869. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 18 December 1869 of Rebecca Tweedie for stealing one coconut mat, the property of Ellen Atkinson.  Tweedie was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for 21 days.  Certificate dated 28 March 1870

title: Bill of indictment: Dorothy Ann Codling
description: Bill of indictment of Dorothy Ann Codling for obtaining 5s from Rachael Bowes by falsely pretending that she (Codling) was cleaning at the house of Hannah Bedlington who lived at Crescent Place in Whitby and who was a neighbour of Bowes.  Codling pretended that Bedlington had sent her to Bowes to ask her to lend 5s or 6s until she (Bedlington) came back from town. Offence committed on 16 November 1867. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment: Jane Lamb
description: Bill of indictment of Jane Lamb for obtaining one stone weight of flour and one pennyworth of yeast from Ann Mackintosh by falsely pretending that she (Lamb) had been sent for the flour and yeast by Mrs Elizabeth Coverdale of the Black Horse Yard at Whitby who would pay later. Offence committed on 6 March 1868. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Mary Ann Lythe
description: Bill of indictment of Mary Ann Lythe for stealing one petticoat, four frocks, one pair of shoes, one jacket, and six pieces of carpet, the property of James Newham. Offence committed on 20 April 1868. Lythe had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 19 November 1867. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 19 November 1867 of Mary Ann Lythe for stealing four jackets and one apron, the property of William Allan.  Lythe was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for 21 days.  Certificate dated 22 June 1868

title: Bill of indictment for misdemeanour: William Ward
description: Bill of indictment of William Ward for keeping and maintaining an ill-governed and disorderly house. Offence committed at the township of Whitby in the parish of Whitby on 27 April 1867. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Mary Ann Jones
description: Bill of indictment of Mary Ann Jones for stealing two boots, the property of John Beadnell. Offence committed on 19 December 1866. Jones had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 9 January 1866. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 9 January 1866 of Mary Ann Jones for stealing one chemise value 1s, the property of Charles Hoggarth, at the township of Whitby on 5 January 1866.  Jones was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for 14 days.  Certificate dated 29 December 1866

title: Bill of indictment: Mary Hannah Fenwick
description: Bill of indictment of Mary Hannah Fenwick for obtaining two boots from George Robinson by falsely pretending that she (Fenwick) had been sent for them by Ann Rookes commonly called Mistress Fletcher who lived in the Post Office Yard in Whitby and who was known to Robinson. Offence committed on 24 June 1867. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment: Jane Corner
description: Bill of indictment of Jane Corner for keeping a disorderly house Offences committed at the township of Whitby on various days since1 June 1867. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony and for receiving stolen goods: Charlotte Boyes
description: Bill of indictment of Charlotte Boyes for stealing one pair of kid gloves, four pairs of stockings, one hair net and one tie, the property of Beckwith Johnson Hopper. Includes indictment of Boyes for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed on 20 May 1866. Boyes had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 5 November 1864. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 5 November 1864 of Charlotte Boyes for stealing one gold ring value 40s, the property of Robert Turner.  Boyes was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for one calendar month.  Certificate dated 2 July 1866

title: Bill of indictment for felony: John Lloyd
description: Bill of indictment of John Lloyd for stealing one jacket, the property of George Auckland. Offence committed on 5 February 1866. Lloyd had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 9 December 1865. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 9 December 1865 of John Lloyd for stealing one copper tea kettle, one brass candlestick, and one clapper of a ship's pump, the property of Thomas Hawxwell.  Lloyd was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for 42 days.  Certificate dated 25 June 1866

title: Bill of indictment: Hannah Jackson
description: Bill of indictment of Hannah Jackson for obtaining ten yards of mohair, another ten yards of mohair, six yards of black lining, and two black mohair aprons from Isaac Busfield by falsely pretending that Mistress Stephenson of Skinner Street in Whitby was her aunt and had sent her to get a mohair dress, ten yards of mohair, six yards of black lining, and two black mohair aprons, and that Mistress Stephenson would call and pay later that evening or on the Monday next following. Offence committed at Whitby on 29 July 1865. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: John Scriven
description: Bill of indictment of John Scriven for stealing one knife, the property of William Dowsland. Offence committed on 29 June 1865. Scriven had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 4 July 1865. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 4 July 1865 of John Scrivins for stealing one pair of boots value 15s, the property of James Jackson.  Scrivins was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for one calendar month.  Certificate dated 10 October 1865

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Lewis Watson
description: Bill of indictment of Lewis Watson for stealing two shirts, two flannel singlets, one rug, one belt, one knife, one sheath, two pairs of drawers, one southwester, two pairs of stockings, three pairs of trousers, one table spoon three tins, one piece of soap, one jacket, and one packet of matches, the property of Scott Morrison and taken from a ship called the "Victory" in the port of Whitby. Offence committed on 9 August 1865. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for misdemeanour: Mary Smith or Waddingham
description: Bill of indictment of Mary Smith otherwise called Mary Waddingham for keeping a disorderly house Offence committed at the township and parish of Whitby on and after 17 October 1863. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Henry Hall
description: Bill of indictment of Henry Hall for stealing one stocking, one purse and 14s 10d in money, the property of Luke Wedgwood. Offence committed on 4 December 1863. Hall had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 14 July 1863. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 14 July 1863 of Henry Hall for stealing one pair of men's strong boots value 10s, the property of Christopher Cooper.  Hall was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for three calendar months.  Certificate dated 2 January 1864

title: Bill of indictment for felony: James Farrow and Thomas Hansill
description: Bill of indictment of James Farrow and Thomas Hansill for stealing eight stones weight of jet value £3 4s, the property of Matthew Coverdale. Offence committed on 4 April 1864. Farrow had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 17 May 1862. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 17 May 1862 of James Farrow for stealing 11 pounds weight of soft jet value 4s 6d, the property of Charles Mark Palmer and others.  Farrow was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for one calendar month.  Certificate dated 5 April 1864

title: Bill of indictment for felony: John Mellor
description: Bill of indictment of John Mellor for stealing one waistcoat, the property of John Eccles. Offence committed on 9 September 1864. Mellor had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 21 May 1859. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 21 May 1859 of John Mellor for stealing two joiner's planes, two chisels, one iron rest and T, one cotton slop, and one calico bag, the property of Matthew Wright.  Mellor was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for two calendar months.  Certificate dated 13 October 1864

title: Bill of indictment: Mary Ann Watson
description: Bill of indictment of Mary Ann Watson for obtaining 5s from William Stockton by falsely pretending that she had a summons from the magistrates in Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 14 February 1863 against him and that it would be served by Hugh MacGregor Superintendent of Police at Whitby. Offence committed on 16 February 1863. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Henry Dickenson and Richard Dickenson
description: Bill of indictment of Henry Dickenson and Richard Dickenson for stealing one piece of canvas, the property of Godfrey Knight. Includes indictment of Henry Dickenson for receiving the stolen goods. Offences committed on 28 May 1863. Henry Dickenson had previously been convicted of felony at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 1 July 1851. Richard Dickinson [sic] had previously been convicted of felony at the Assizes and General Gaol Delivery for the county of York held at the Castle of York on 7 March 1855. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"With certificate of conviction at the Quarter Sessions held at Northallerton on 1 July 1851 of Henry Dickinson late of the House of Correction at Northallerton for stealing 16 hams and 25 stones weight of ham, the property of Robert Sawdon.  Dickinson was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for six calendar months.  Certificate dated 29 June 1863. With certificate of conviction at the Assizes and General Gaol Delivery for the county of York held at the Castle of York on 7 March 1855 of Richard Dickinson for breaking into the dwelling house of James Appleby at the parish of Whitby on 30 September 1854 and stealing 12 silver watches and one gold ring, the property of the said James Appleby.  Dickinson, who had a previous conviction for felony, was sentenced to penal servitude for four years.  Certificate dated 29 June 1863

title: Bill of indictment for felony: Esther Knaggs
description: Bill of indictment of Esther Knaggs for stealing one silver watch and one watch chain, the property of William Currie,Offence committed on 15 April 1863. Knaggs had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 22 December 1860. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "a true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 22 December 1860 of Esther Knaggs for stealing three stones weight of coal value 3d, the property of John Anderson.  Knaggs was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for 14 days.  Certificate dated 26 June 1863

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Greenwood and Robert Pennock
description: Bill of indictment of William Greenwood and Robert Pennock for stealing two towels, six dish cloths, two pounds weight of mutton, one jacket, one bone mustard spoon, and one hedge slasher, the property of William Lloyd. Includes indictment of Pennock for receiving the stolen goods. Offence committed on 2 December 1861. Greenwood had previously been convicted of felony at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 29 December 1857. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"With certificate of conviction at a Petty Sessions held at Whitby on 29 December 1857 of William Greenwood for attempting to steal 14s in money, the property of William Mead.  Greenwood was sentenced to hard labour at the House of Correction at Northallerton for two calendar months  Certificate dated 30 December 1861

title: Bill of indictment: Hannah Banks
description: Bill of indictment of Hannah Banks for obtaining one shawl from Edmund Crane a draper at Whitby by falsely pretending that she had been sent by Mistress Wilson wife of Thomas Wilson of Bridge Street in Whitby grocer to take a shawl to Wilson's house for his wife who would then call at the draper's the next day to pay for it. Offence committed on 24 July 1862. Endorsed with names of witnesses and "true bill"

title: Bill of indictment for misdemeanour: Thomas Smith
description: Bill of indictment of Thomas Smith for obtaining one sixpenny loaf of bread, one quarter of a pound of tea, two ounces of tobacco, one half pound of candles and one pound of lump sugar from Ann Forrest by falsely pretending to have been sent for the goods by William Ellison of Baxtergate in the township of Whitby shoemaker, who was known to Ann Forrest and a customer of her husband Francis in his business as a grocer and provision dealer Offence committed on 4 October 1861. title: Midsummer Quarter Sessions: records of summary convictions

Four inquests are listed:- George Stephenson.  Inquest held at Hawsker cum Stainsacre on 15 July 1818.  Verdict: accidentally killed- Edward Wilson.  Inquest held at Whitby on 14 August 1818.  Verdict: visitation of God- Joseph Mennell.  Inquest held at Whitby on 14 August 1818.  Verdict: accidental- James Brown.  Inquest held at Whitby on 22 September 1818.  Verdict: visitation of God

title: Abstract of coroner's inquests for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand
description: An abstract of inquisitions taken by Henry Belcher gentleman coroner for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand and given in at the Lent Assizes 1819 held at the Castle of York. Three inquests are listed:- John Marshall.  Inquest held at Whitby on 6 January 1819.  Verdict: accidentally killed- Mary Coulston.  Inquest held at Whitby on 12 January 1819.  Verdict: visitation of God- Martha Atkinson.  Inquest held at Whitby on 1 March 1819.  Verdict: accidental death

title: Settlement examination: Dennis Downes
description: Examination of Dennis Downes who says he was born at Cork in Ireland where he lived until he was 11 years old. He then enlisted in the Marines and served for three years, mainly on shore in Plymouth.  He was put on board the Standard a 64 [gun vessel] and served under Captain Ellison for 21/2 years during which time he lost his left leg below the knee.  He was sent to a hospital near Portsmouth and was discharged from the service.  He was then sent to St Thomas' Hospital by order of the Sick and Wounded Office, and stayed there for three or four months.  About nine or ten months afterwards, on 18 September 1797, he was married at Manchester.  In the summer of 1798, he was taken up at Whitby and committed to the House of Correction at Northallerton as a rogue and vagabond, together with his wife Grace Denis.  He was discharged at the next Midsummer Sessions and since then he has been wandering round in Scotland and the North of England with his wife and children begging and selling godly books.  On 16 October he was found begging and apprehended near the town of Snainton

title: Notice of an appeal for a return of duties on salt lost at sea
description: Notice from John Watkinson to J. Berry esquire Collector of Excise for Whitby relating to the loss of 188 bushels of refined salt shipped at Hull on 5 December 1799 on board the sloop Friendship (Nathaniel Burstall master) by Thomas Nesbitt.  The salt was made by Crosbie and Urmson of Frodsham in Cheshire makers and refiners, and consigned to John Watkinson, Richard Bellwood, William Wood, Samuel Middleton and Eustace Cass all of Scarborough.  On 1 January 1800 the sloop sailed to Scarborough, but was overtaken by a violent storm which drove her on shore near Scarborough where she filled with water and all the salt was lost. On 6 December George Hopwood shipped 179 bushels of refined salt on board the sloop Friendship (Nathaniel Burstall master), the salt having been made by Twiss, Morris and Co of Wheelock Saltworks near Sandbach in Cheshire makers and refiners, and consigned to Messrs Skelton and Paylor, Peter Marshall, Isabella White and William Clarkson all of Scarborough and by the aforesaid accident 153 bushels of salt were lost. The matter will be determined at the Quarter Sessions to be held at New Malton on 14 January 1800

title: Notice relating to salt lost at sea
description: Notice to the Commissioners of Excise and the Collector of Excise at Whitby given by John Marshall on behalf of Christopher Richardson of Whitby esquire. On 16 April 1800 1,145 bushels and five pounds of white salt consigned to Richardson by Messrs Crosbie and Urmson of Liverpool in Lancashire makers or refiners of salt was put on board the sloop Venus of Liverpool (Thomas Burton master) and the duty was paid.  Between 11 and 12 o'clock at night on 18 May 1800 they were coming into the harbour at Whitby but were prevented by a rope stretched across the harbour from the West Pier to a brig called the Happy Return of Whitby, which was in danger of drifting to the south of the harbour onto the rock.  Soon afterwards, the rope broke and the Venus and the Happy Return became entangled and drifted and were cast behind the East Pier and struck on the rocks. The woman with him is Marianne his wife, but he does not know either his or her place of settlement- George Fenley a sailor without a pass who does not know if he has any settlement- Jane Wilson a widow who travels to earn her livelihood.  She has no pass and believes that she is settled at Bishop Auckland in county Durham - Elizabeth Wilkinson wife of Richard Wilkinson a chimney sweeper.  She does not know his settlement and believes her maiden settlement was at Berwick. Elizabeth Wilkinson alias Harbottle wife of John Wilkinson. title: Petition of the inhabitants of Fylingdales
description: Petition to the Justices from the minister, churchwardens and major part of the inhabitants of the parish of Fylingdales.  Their church had become decayed and despite efforts to preserve it, it had to be demolished and rebuilt.  On 15 October 1816 the petitioners applied to the Justices who, after James Peacock stonemason and Gideon Smailes joiner, both able and experienced workmen of Whitby, estimated the cost of repair at £885 18s, certified this to the Lord Chancellor so that they could obtain letters patent.  Following this the churchwardens received £109, which together with a further £215, has been paid to workmen rebuilding the church.   They now ask the Justices to certify the facts again, so that another brief may be obtained. Signed by the minister, churchwardens and 33 inhabitants

title: Annual return of lunatics: Whitby Union
description: Annual return of lunatics in the Whitby Union, giving names, ages, parish to which chargeable, where maintained, weekly cost of maintenance, whether lunatic or idiot, dangerous to himself or others, of dirty habits, how long they have been of unsound mind, and observations.  Includes:- Ann Corney aged 53 years, chargeable to Aislaby, and sent to the York Asylum in 1839.  Her weekly cost of maintenance is 7s 6d; she is a lunatic, dangerous to herself, of dirty habits, and has been of unsound mind for five years- Ellen Stonehouse aged 63 years, chargeable to Newholm with Dunsley, and sent to the York Asylum in 1831.  Her weekly cost of maintenance is 7s 6d; she is a lunatic, dangerous to others at times, not of dirty habits, and has been of unsound mind for 13 years.  She is "rather improved" of late years- Elizabeth Lincoln aged 31 years, chargeable to Ruswarp, and sent to the York Asylum in 1837.  Her weekly cost of maintenance is 7s 6d; she is a lunatic, dangerous to others, of dirty habits, and has been of unsound mind for ten years.  She is subject to fits of furious phrenzy [sic]- John Hunter aged 37 years, chargeable to Whitby, and sent to the Gate Helmsley Retreat in 1836.  His weekly cost of maintenance is 8s 2d; he is a lunatic, occasionally dangerous to himself or others, not of dirty habits, and has been of unsound mind for nine years.  He is liable to sudden gusts of maniacal fury- Jane Yeoman aged 27 years, chargeable to Whitby, and sent to the Gate Helmsley Retreat in 1840.  Her weekly cost of maintenance is 8s 2d; she is a lunatic, dangerous to herself and others, of dirty habits, and has been of unsound mind for five years- Mary Turner aged 37 years, chargeable to Ruswarp, and sent to the Gate Helmsley Retreat in 1839.  Her weekly cost of maintenance is 8s 2d; she is a lunatic, not dangerous to herself or others, not of dirty habits, and has been of unsound mind for five years.  She is a monomaniac- Robinson Stonehouse aged 30 years, chargeable to Lythe, and sent to the Gate Helmsley Retreat in 1839.  His weekly cost of maintenance is 8s 2d; he is a lunatic, occasionally dangerous to himself or others, not of dirty habits, and has been of unsound mind for six years.  He is subject to sudden gusts of maniacal fury- William Harland aged 41 years, chargeable to Lythe.  His weekly cost of maintenance is 2s 6d; he is an idiot, not dangerous to himself or others, of dirty habits , and has been of unsound mind all his life

title: Settlement examination: James Reed
description: Settlement examination of James Reed a vagrant.  At about Michaelmas last, he left Scotland to travel to Newcastle, and from there to York through Durham via Darlington, Northallerton and other towns.  From York he was returning to Scotland when he was apprehended at Marske in Cleveland.  He had travelled from York through Malton, Scarborough and Whitby and other towns on or near the coast.  During this time, he maintained himself for five or six years by selling godly and other small books.  Before then, he had been a weaver in Glasgow, but could not continue because of lameness and infirmities

title: Settlement examination: John Watson
description: Settlement examination of John Watson a vagrant.  About five or six months ago, he set off from Burlington in the North Riding to York.  He stayed in or around York for about a month, and then went via Scarborough, Whitby, Staithes and other places near the coast, to Marske in Cleveland, where he was apprehended.  He has maintained himself by begging.  He met James Reed at Staithes, and they travelled together to Skelton.  Before he left Burlington, he supported himself by begging.  He was born at Burlington, and believes that his father gained a settlement there

She should have received ten days' notice.  Also William Gardiner is now in York Castle for a debt and so cannot appear to plead guilty or not guilty. title: Letters and papers relating to the alteration of highway districts
description: Letters and papers relating to the alteration of highway districts, including:- printed copy of the final order for the division of the Riding into Highway Districts, made at the Michaelmas Sessions 1867- letter dated 28 October 1867 from Robert Pearson at Helmsley to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Northallerton, pointing out the omission of Snilesworth from the Ryedale district, as published in the York papers on Saturday last- letter dated 15 November 1867 from Robert Pearson at the County Courts' Registrar's Office at Helmsley to T.T. Trevor esquire.  Snilesworth is assessed for the county rate to the division of Birdforth.  It was formerly joined with Bilsdale West Side, but was separated by an order of Quarter Sessions.  It was probably intended to include Snilesworth in the Ryedale Highway District- letter dated 3 December 1867 from John Richardson at Thirsk to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Northallerton.  Sinderby, which is in the Thirsk Poor law Union and adjoins Ainderby Quernhow and Pickhill, appears to have been accidentally omitted from the published list of Birdforth- notice dated 1 January 1868 given to the Clerk of the Peace by five Justices that a proposal will be made at the next Quarter Sessions to remove the township of Barforth from the Richmond Highway District and to include it in the Greta Bridge Highway District- undated petition of the ratepayers of the township of Barforth to remain in Richmond Highway District and not to be added to the Greta Bridge Highway District- letter dated 13 January 1868 from John Teale at Leyburn clerk to the Leyburn Highway District to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Northallerton relating to alterations in the Leyburn Highway District to be comprised in the provisional order at the next Easter Sessions- letter dated 16 January 1868 from W.O. Woodall acting clerk for the Pickering Lythe East Highway Board at 26 Queen Street, Scarborough, to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Northallerton.  The highway township of Everley should be separated from the highway township of Suffield.  The present waywarden will act for both places until the separation is made, when separate waywardens will be elected for each township- letter dated 18 January 1868 from George A. Herring clerk to the Hang East Highway Board at Bedale to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Northallerton, giving alterations in the district of Hang East affecting Rand and Swainby with Allerthorpe- letter dated 20 January 1868 from Isaiah Wilkinson clerk to the Whitby Strand Highway Board to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Northallerton.  No alterations in any of the townships are necessary or desirable- letter dated 21 January 1868 from W.O. Woodall acting clerk of the Highway Board at 26 Queen Street, Scarborough, to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Northallerton.  Everley is not a township maintaining its own poor.  If Langdale End and Wykeham have been separated in the final order, then so to should have been Suffield and Everley- letter dated 25 January 1868 from Samuel Walker clerk to the Malton [Highway] Board to T.T. Trevor esquire relating to the omission of the township of Hildenley from the final order.  Hildenley has no highways but has a public bridleway which it is bound to maintain.  The township of Crambe should be removed from the Bulmer East Highway District, and the township of Scackleton should be removed from the Bulmer West Highway District, and both should be added to the Malton District- letter dated 27 January 1868 from John Richardson at Thirsk to T.T. Trevor esquire.  The townships of Sinderby and Sowerby, were accidentally omitted, but should form part of the Birdforth Highway District- letter dated 28 January 1868 from Robert Pearson of the Ryedale Highway Board at Helmsley to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Northallerton suggesting alterations in the townships comprising the Ryedale district- letter dated 1 February 1868 from George A. Herring at Bedale to T.T. Trevor deputy Clerk of the Peace at Guisborough.  The Hang East Highway Board came to no resolution relating to the township of Swainby with Allerthorpe, which is included in the Hang East District.  At the first meeting of the Highway Board, the inhabitants stated that they had no roads in the township and had therefore not thought it necessary to appoint a waywarden.  If the township is liable to contribute to the common fund of the district, then they should appoint a waywarden- letter dated 1 February 1868 from W.O. Woodall acting clerk at Scarborough to T.T. Trevor esquire at Guisborough.  The precepts for Wykeham and Langdale End should in both cases be addressed to the waywardens.  It would be advisable for [Langdale End] township to be included in Wykeham, as it belongs to that parish. The Justices should have no difficulty ascertaining which townships maintained their own poor and which did not- letter dated 1 February 1868 from Robert Pearson clerk to the Ryedale Highway Board at Helmsley to T.T. Trevor esquire.  "Morton" is the correct spelling for the township, which maintains its own poor and forms part of the Helmsley Poor Law Union.  It is in the division of Birdforth, and he believes it to be extra-parochial- letter dated 4 February 1868 from George A. Herring at Bedale to T.T. Trevor solicitor at Guisborough.  The township of Swainby is no doubt the same place as Swainby with Allerthorpe.  He quotes Langdale's "Dictionary of the North Riding" to support this, and says that in the Bedale Union it is called Swainby with Allerthorpe- letter dated 12 February 1868 from George A. Herring clerk at Bedale to T.T. Trevor esquire at Northallerton, containing the resolution of the Hang East Highway Board relating to Swainby with Allerthorpe and Ainderby Myers with Holtby- letter dated 17 February 1868 from George Legard of Easthorpe, Malton, to Mr Walker giving his apologies for not attending the Highway Committee on Wednesday next.  Gives details of matters to be brought before the committee relating to the Malton district- letter dated 18 February 1868 from James Pulleine at Darlington Station.  He is on his way from Berwick with a bad cold, and may be unable to appear at Northallerton tomorrow, but he has asked for the resolutions of the Bedale Board of Waywardens to be sent there.  The Board decided that townships having no roads should appoint waywardens to pay their proportion of establishment charges.  This may necessitate the division of townships that are otherwise joined- letter dated 18 February 1868 from George A. Herring clerk at Bedale to James Pulleine, care of Mr Trevor at Northallerton, headed "Hang East Highway Board".  He has sent Mr Trevor the resolutions of the last meeting of the Board relating to Swainby and Ainderby Myers with Holtby.  Christopher Bell, who occupies two farms under Mr Milbank, has called on him relating to Thorp being separated from Snape for highway purposes- notice dated 19 February 1868 given to the Clerk of the Peace by five Justices that at the next Sessions alterations (as listed) will be proposed to the final order made at the Michaelmas Sessions 1867 relating to the division of the Riding into highway districts; with draft- letter dated 24 February 1868 from John Richardson at Thirsk to T.T. Trevor esquire relating to Birdforth Highway District.  There is no such place as Ampleforth, but there are places called Ampleforth Birdforth, Ampleforth St Peter and Ampleforth Oswaldkirk Quarter which are all allotted to other districts.  The word Ampleforth should therefore be removed from the district of Birdforth- letter dated 26 March 1868 from Robert R. Blyth for the Bulmer East Highway Board at York to T.T. Trevor solicitor at Guisborough asking how to proceed, as a township in his division is annexed to another township for the purposes of the Act [relating to Highway Boards], but wishes to stand alone- letter dated 30 March 1868 from Robert R. Blyth for the Bulmer East Highway Board at York to T.T. Trevor esquire giving the reasons for the wish of the inhabitants of Cornbrough to be separate from Sheriff Hutton for highway purposes and to have a waywarden of their own- letter dated 30 March 1868 from Robert R. Blyth for the Bulmer East Highway Board at York to T.T. Trevor solicitor at Guisborough relating to altering the Highway District for Bulmer East division by severing two townships- printed copy of the provisional order for the alteration of highway districts made at Quarter Sessions on 7 April 1868- copy of The London Gazette dated 7 July 1868 containing a copy of the final order for the alteration of Highway Districts made at the Quarter Sessions held on 30 June 1868

title: Papers relating to a sentence imposed on Richard Collier of Whitby
description: Papers relating to a sentence imposed on Richard Collier, including:- petition dated March 1867 of ratepayers and inhabitants of the town of Whitby who are acquainted with Richard Collier of Whitby jet worker, who had been sentenced to 12 months imprisonment for assaulting John Dearlove.  They ask that Collier's sentence should be mitigated, as Dearlove was a brothel keeper who fancied that his wife was too intimate with Collier, and because a stone was thrown at Dearlove by his own wife and not by Collier.  The petitioners are well aware of Collier's intemperance, but consider him an honest and well-disposed man.  Signed by 61 inhabitants- letter dated 1 April 1867 from Mary Ann Collier, Richard Collier's mother, at Baxtergate in Whitby, asking the Chairman to use his influence on her behalf

title: Alterations to the rules of the Whitby Marine Society
description: Copy of the alterations made to the articles of the Whitby Marine Society, as allowed by the Justices at Northallerton on 2 October 1798. At the annual meeting held on 3 January 1798 it was resolved that no member should be free of the club and no money shall be taken out of the box or fund before 1 January 1799.  If before then, any member would have been entitled to an allowance from the Club had this rule not been made, then he should be paid a sum not exceeding £10. Signed by James Harrison, Richard Hutchinson, James Watt, R.Bd Moorsom, Richard Cook, and Marmaduke Wilson

title: Memorial relating to Whitby Bridge
description: Memorial to the Justices from the merchants, tradesmen and inhabitants of Whitby relating to the inconvenience caused by the opening of the bridge.  The bridgemen are paid partly by the county, but mainly by fees collected from craft using the Bridgeway, which leads them to regard the entrance of any craft paying a toll as of the first importance, and causes delays to people and traffic using the bridge.  Every branch of trade should be encouraged, especially the herring fishing, which is so important and beneficial to Whitby.  The petitioners wish the bridge to be placed under efficient control that would make the bridgemen less dependent on entrance fees without inconveniencing the herring fishing. Signed by 253 inhabitants, giving name, occupation and residence

title: Papers relating to C.A. Crigan's summons as a juror
description: Certificate dated 29 July [sic] 1866 of G.H. Holtby physician etc at Whitby that C.A. Crigan esquire occasionally suffers from palpitations of the heart and difficulty of breathing, and should not be confined in a crowded court at this time of the year. Letter dated 2 July 1866 from John Topham to Charles Crigan of Sleights Hall near Whitby, returning the above certificate.  Topham is unable to excuse Mr Crigan's attendance, as he is summoned for the Grand Jury rather than the Traverse Jury, and will only be in court for about half an hour in the early part of the morning. Note dated 4 July from Charles Crigan at Northallerton.  He only received "the enclosed" late last night as has come on the first train this morning.  He is suffering from an attack of neuralgia, and if his presence is not needed in court, as he hears that the Grand Jury will be dismissed this morning, then he would like to return home by the evening train, as he is far from well

He had on a pepper and salt coloured mixture coat, with a black waistcoat, striped corded breeches, and boots, and had a white silk handkerchief, and was wearing a watch.  He had with him a small bundle, and when apprehended he was mounted upon a good dark bay blood mare. Endorsed "Mr Hirst wants Mr Butler's order for his theatre at Whitby- order dated 29 September 1797 to the constable of Hawes to take Daniel Skinner late of Grantham in Lincolnshire yeoman to the House of Correction at Northallerton, and to the Keeper of the House of Correction to receive him.
