title: Papers relating to a gunpowder magazine at Barnby
description: Papers relating to an application to erect a gunpowder magazine at Barnby, including:- draft notice dated 13 June 1857 given by John Greene, agent for James Merricks of the Roslin Powder Mills in North Britain, to the churchwardens and overseers of the township of Barnby in the parish of Lythe.  Greene intends to apply at the next Quarter Sessions for a licence for a gunpowder magazine to be built on ground belonging to John Corner junior of Whitby, and contracted to be sold to Merricks.  The land lies in the township of Barnby in the parish of Lythe, bounded by land of the Marquis of Normanby on the north, by the highway on the east and south, and by land of William Eccles on the west- copy notice dated 30 June 1857 similar to the above- letter dated 26 June 1857 from G.?J. Kenmir at Wellington Street, High Level Bridge End, Gateshead, to T.T. Trevor esquire, relating to the application for the licence.  The magazine will be in the centre of a district where large quantities of gunpowder are used, but the site is quite isolated.  It is about a mile and a half from Mulgrave Castle, but the Marquis of Normanby supports the application- brief for the applicant dated 30 June 1857 at the Midsummer Sessions, containing a copy notice dated 13 June 1857, the case made by James Merricks of the firm of Hay, Merricks and Company of the Roslin Gunpowder Mills near Edinburgh, and proofs- letter dated 6 July 1857 from G.?J. Kenmir at Wellington Street, High Level Bridge End, Gateshead, to T.T. Trevor esquire solicitor at Guisborough, asking him to send the licence that was granted at the last Sessions.  Asks for a list of others with similar licences in the North Riding.  Endorsed with pencilled list: Thomas Brentnall at Eston; John Greene of Morton, the said John Greene of Lazenby; John Coldwells of Staithes; David Baker of Pinchinthorpe; and James Merricks of Barnby

title: Papers relating to an appeal against the removal of Robert Witty, his wife and family
description: Papers relating to an appeal against the removal of Robert Witty, his wife and family, including:- copy order dated 14 June 1842 for the removal of Robert Witty, Ann his wife, and their children Mary Ann and Matthew, from the township of Ruswarp to the parish of Selby in the West Riding.  Includes:i) settlement examination dated 14 June 1842 of Robert Witty of the township of Ruswarp weaver.  He is 59 years old.  About 45 years ago, his parents lived in Selby.  When he was 16 years old, he was apprenticed for five years to John Twist of Selby sail cloth manufacturer.  His father Matthew Witty was a party to the apprenticeship indenture.  During his apprenticeship, he slept in Millgate Street in Selby, in his father's house.  After two and a half years, he quarrelled with his master and it was agreed to cancel the apprenticeship indenture, which was burnt in his presence.  About 20 years ago, as Witty was out of work, he applied to the overseers of Selby for relief and received 1s a day for four days.  His settlement was examined by a committee at Selby workhouse, and was found to be in the parish of Selby, and he then received 15s relief.  About five years ago he married Ann at Whitby and has two children, Mary Ann aged 18 months and Matthew aged three weeks.  He has done nothing to gain a settlement elsewhere, although he is now living with his wife and children in the township of Ruswarp, and chargeable to that townshipii) notice of chargeability dated 15 June 1842 given by the overseers of the township of Ruswarp to the overseers of the parish of Selby- copy notice dated 1 July 1842 given to the overseers of the township of Ruswarp by the churchwardens and overseers of the parish of Selby of their intention to prosecute the appeal against the removal of Robert Witty and his family- brief for the appellants in the appeal at the Michaelmas Sessions on 18 October 1842 relating to the removal of Robert Witty, his wife and family- bill of expenses of Newstead and Richardson with the overseers of Selby relating to work done on their behalf between June 1842 and October 1842 relating to the settlement of Robert Witty and his family

title: Letter relating to John Calvert as inspector of weights and balances
description: Letter from Jonas Brown at Newton House to Thomas Ewbank at Malton relating to the appointment of John Calvert as inspector of weights and balances in the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand.  When Calvert attended the last Quarter Sessions to be sworn in, he was told that an Act of Parliament appointed the Chief Constable or any other persons that he might depute.  Calvert was therefore not sworn in.  Had Brown been told of this, he would have attended the Sessions, although his health was then precarious and he was nearly 80 years old, and unable to travel in the inclement weather.  Calvert is the person that he would recommend and depute; he is an honest man and stands high in the estimation of those for whom he receives rents and transacts business. A set of standard weights has been sent to Whitby.  They will be heavy and may need to be carried in a cart with two horses and two men.  The townships are about 25 miles apart at the extremities, and the roads are very rugged and indifferent[This document was found in the bundle of papers for Michaelmas 1809]

description: An account the expenses of William Dinsdale of Aiskew coroner for holding inquests from July to October 1839; with receipts for individual expenses. Inquest held at Osmotherley on 6 July 1839.  Verdict: by the visitation of God- Ann Hammond aged 79 years.  Inquest held at Carlton on 12 July 1839.  Verdict: by the visitation of God- Sarah Shaw aged 7 years.  Inquest held at Langthorpe on 14 July 1839.  Verdict: drowned accidentally- Elizabeth Coghlan aged 76 years. Verdict: from natural causes- Thomas Robinson aged 38 years.  Inquest held at Arkengarthdale on 5 August 1839.  Verdict: accidentally killed- Richard Akers aged 21 years. Verdict: by the visitation of God- Robert Webster aged 32 years.  Inquest held at Leyburn on 31 August 1839.  Verdict: accidentally scalded to death- Mary Cleasby aged 31 years.  Inquest held at Arkengarthdale on 4 September 1839.  Verdict: by the visitation of God- John Sutherland aged 15 weeks.  Inquest held at Whitby on 7 September 1839.  Verdict: accidentally suffocated- Thomas Plummer aged 28 years.  Inquest held at Lunedale on 19 September 1839.  Verdict: died from the inclemency of the weather- Elizabeth Sweeting aged 21 years.  Inquest held at Whitby on 24 September 1839.  Verdict: the deceased came to her death in consequence of too early removal from York after her confinement of a male child being at the same time under a suspended order of removal from the parish of St Olave - Elizabeth Brewster aged 74 years.  Inquest held at Kepwick on 26 September 1839.  Verdict: by the visitation of God- Jane Suggett aged 78 years.  Inquest held at Brompton on 2 October 1839.  Verdict: by the visitation of God- John Walker aged 73 years.  Inquest held at Scargill on 6 October 1839.  Verdict: by the visitation of God- Jane Broadley aged 4 years.  Inquest held at Ellingstring on 8 October 1839.  Verdict: accidentally burnt- Leonard Eden aged 48 years.  Inquest held at Thirsk on 9 October 1839.  Verdict: by the visitation of God- Ann Smith aged 84 years.  Inquest held at Colburn on 10 October 1839.  Verdict: accidentally burnt- Alexander Shepherd aged 1 year. title: Records relating to the removal of Thomas Carling
description: Order dated 9 April 1793 made in the appeal between the inhabitants of Lythe (appellants) and the inhabitants of Whitby (respondents) relating to the removal of Thomas Carling from Whitby to Lythe.  Carling was the son of William and Mary Carling and was born in Lythe.  Before his marriage and a few days after Martinmas 1731, William Carling was in the service of Matthew Campion at the township of Barnby as a servant of husbandry and was there for over a year.  Campion, long since dead, had said that William Carling (now also dead) had been hired for a year but the court refused to admit this evidence.  The order of removal was confirmed. Writ dated 7 May 1793 requiring any orders made relating to the removal of Thomas Carling to be returned to the court of King's Bench. Order dated 8 June 1793 that the removal order returned with the writ of certiorari should be sent back to the Sessions to be restated

title: Brief for an appeal relating to the removal of Elizabeth Wetherill and her daughter

In support of this order Marske will prove that Elizabeth's settlement was at Potto before her marriage to John Weatherill. Potto will show that John Weatherill was born at Swainby, the place of his father's settlement, with evidence from Amelia Weatherill his mother.  Elizabeth Weatherill will prove her marriage at Whitby, although as she is being removed by the name Weatherill, this may not be necessary

title: Abstract of inquisitions taken by John Buchannan
description: An abstract of inquisitions taken by John Buchannan one of the coroners for the North Riding between 28 March 1860 and June 1860.  With vouchers for the expenses of holding the inquests. Six inquests are listed:- Elizabeth Helm Pearson.  Inquest held at the house of Job Wardell (the sign of the Crown and Anchor) in the township of Whitby on 5 April 1860.  Verdict: suffocated by eating suet dumpling whilst labouring under whooping cough- William Ward.  Inquest held at the house of Robert Stratford (the Custom House Coffee House) in the township of Whitby on 11 April 1860.  Verdict: killed by accidentally falling from the rigging upon the deck of the Brig "Active" of Whitby- John Parkes.  Inquest held at the house of William Perry (the Tunnel Inn), in the township of Eskdaleside on 28 April 1860.  Verdict: accidentally killed by being crushed between two tubs of ironstone in an ironstone mine- a newly-born female child, name unknown.  Inquest held at the Justice Room in Whitby on 7 May 1860.  Verdict: wilful murder against some person or persons unknown- Mark Laidley.  Inquest held at the house of George Wastell (the Britannia Inn) in the township of Whitby on 2 June 1860.  Verdict: accidentally killed by being thrown from a perambulator against the wheels of a cart- Henry Pickett.  Inquest held at the house of John Walker (the Neptune Inn) in the township of Whitby on 7 June 1860.  Verdict: accidentally killed by falling from the fore yard to the deck of the brig "Griffin" of Southampton

description: Letter from Richard Trenam sheriff's officer at Nawton near Helmsley to Mr Shepherd deputy governor at the gaol at Northallerton.  Trenam asks Shepherd to engage his brother or some other respectable person to do his duty as bailiff.  He is unable to attend as he has other business in hand.  He has just returned from Burlington and has to set off for Whitby with warrants from the Court of Exchequer that he has to execute on or before Wednesday next.  Trenam would have sent his son, but the son has had an eruption of a blood vessel on his lungs and has not been able to get out of the house for the last ten weeks

title: Certificate of returns of corn and oatmeal: Whitby

title: Abstract of coroner's inquests for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand
description: An abstract of inquisitions taken by Henry Belcher gentleman coroner for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand and given in at the Lent Assizes 1821 held at the Castle of York. Eight inquests are listed:- Thomas Benson.  Inquest held at Whitby on 24 July 1820.  Verdict: accidentally drowned- Philip Hoggart.  Inquest held at Stoupe Brow on 13 August 1820.  Verdict: accidental death- William Hill.  Inquest held at Ugglebarnby on 20 November 1820.  Verdict: visitation of God- John Abram.  Inquest held at Whitby on 24 November 1820.  Verdict: visitation of God- John Noddings.  Inquest held at Whitby on 30 November 1820.  Verdict: excessive drinking- Lawrence Jackson.  Inquest held at Upgang on 8 December 1820.  Verdict: found drowned- Elizabeth Madders.  Inquest held at Whitby on 11 February 1821.  Verdict: visitation of God- Thomas Robinson.  Inquest held at Whitby on 17 February 1821.  Verdict: visitation of God

Recognizance made by William Wilkinson of the township of Whitby high constable for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to give evidence in the case against John Dixon. Recognizance made by William Wilkinson of the township of Whitby high constable for the appearance of John Robinson of Barnby at the next Quarter Sessions to give evidence in the case against John Dixon. Recognizance made by William Wilkinson of the township of Whitby high constable for the appearance of Francis Hodgson of the township of Roxby labourer at the next Quarter Sessions to give evidence in the case against John Dixon

title: Recognizance for John Humphrey of Whitby to appear and answer

title: Evidence in the case against Elizabeth Sedman
description: Depositions of John Bedlington Rickinson of the township of Whitby grocer, Thomas Garbutt his apprentice, William Wilkinson the elder of Whitby high constable, witnesses in the case against Elizabeth Sedman; and statement of Elizabeth Sedman, the accused

title: Evidence in the case against John Reed
description: Depositions of James Boanas of the township of Whitby gardener, William Wilkinson the younger of Whitby constable, Thomas Linskill of Whitby policemen, witnesses in the case against John Reed; and statement of John Reed, the accused

title: Evidence in the case against John Reed
description: Depositions of George Miller innkeeper and Philip Hoggarth policeman, both of the township of Whitby, and William Wilkinson the younger of Whitby constable, witnesses in the case against John Reed; and statement of John Reed, the accused

title: Evidence in the case against John Wildon
description: Depositions of George Miller innkeeper and Richard Rayne the younger mariner, both of the township of Whitby, witnesses in the case against John Wildon; and statement of John Wildon the accused

title: Evidence in the case against Richard Rayne and William Harker
description: Depositions of William Marwood of the township of Whitby gentleman, and John Reed blacksmith, Thomas Linskill constable, and William Wilkinson the younger constable, all of Whitby, witnesses in the case against Richard Rayne and William Harker; and statement of Rayne and Harker the accused

title: Evidence in the case against John Dixon and Jane Dixon
description: Depositions of Thomas Trattles of the township of Hinderwell fishmonger, Robert Rosamond of the township of Lythe constable, James Dickinson of Great Moorsholm fishmonger, William Wilkinson of Whitby high constable, James Pennock of Limber Hill in the township of Egton farmer, Jane Jefferson wife of William Jefferson labourer and Jane Brough wife of Joseph Brough labourer, both of Egton, Ann Tyerman widow and Susannah Unthank spinster, both of Staithes, witnesses in the case against John Dixon and Jane Dixon; and statement of John Dixon and Jane Dixon, the accused

title: Evidence in the case against Robert Fothergill

title: Evidence in the case against John Humphrey
description: Depositions of Francis Addison of the township of Whitby innkeeper, Robert Ventriss labourer, John Gardiner labourer, George Lockey dealer in marine stores, and William Wilkinson the younger constable, all of Whitby, witnesses in the case against John Humphrey

title: The Clerk of the Peace's accounts
description: Summary of the Clerk of the Peace's accounts for the quarter, as examined by the Finance Committee.  The committee have also audited the Chief Constables' accounts for precepts, the accounts for Yarm Bridge rents, the account of the Clerk to the Visitors of Private Lunatic Asylums, and the account of the returning officer for the borough of Whitby under the Register of Voters Act. Second summary, presumably from a different Sessions, confirming that the chief constables' accounts for precepts have also been audited

title: Chief constable's bill for precepts: Whitby Strand division
description: Bill of expenses of William Wilkinson chief constable for the division of Whitby Strand for precepts issued since the Midsummer Sessions 1845 relating to hearing appeals against the poor rates, lists of jurors, brewster sessions, brewster transfers, and payment of the county rate

title: Papers relating to the inspection of weights and measures: Whitby Strand division
description: Papers relating to the inspection of weights and measures in the division of Whitby Strand, including:- order dated 30 August 1845 for William Wilkinson the elder, high constable of the division of Whitby Strand, having been appointed as examiner of weights, measures and balances for the division of Whitby Strand, to examine weights and measures in the division of Whitby Strand- order dated 11 October 1845 from two magistrates for the division of Whitby Strand to the Treasurer of the North Riding to pay William Wilkinson and his assistant for examining weights, measures and balances from 1 September 1845 to 11 October 1845 - bill of expenses of William Wilkinson for stamping weights in Whitby Strand

title: Bill of expenses of the returning officer for the borough of Whitby
description: Bill of expenses of the returning officer for the borough of Whitby between June 1845 and October 1845, including the number of voters in each township in the borough; with voucher from R. Kirby returning officer for advertisements of barrister's court and for lists of borough voters

title: Abstract of coroner's inquests for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand
description: An abstract of inquisitions taken by John Buchannan gentleman coroner for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand and given in at the Summer Assizes 1845.  With account of expenses of holding inquests and receipts for expenses for each inquest. Four inquests are listed:- James Lund.  Inquest held at Whitby on 17 March 1845.  Verdict: died by the visitation of God of apoplexy- Isabella Batt.  Inquest held at Whitby on 20 March 1845.  Verdict: died by the visitation of God of disease of the heart- Ann Harrison.  Inquest held at Fylingdales on 24 March 1845.  Verdict: died by the visitation of God of apoplexy- Robert Trueman Dale.  Inquest held at Whitby on 10 June 1845.  Verdict: accidental death by drowning

title: Order to pay the constable of Whitby
description: Order to the Chief Constable of the North Riding or the Treasurer to pay a reward to William Robinson constable of Whitby for apprehending Charles Langdale and Margaret Langdale rogues and vagabonds found wandering in the parish of Whitby. Order to the Chief Constable of the North Riding or the Treasurer to pay William Robinson constable of Whitby his expenses for conveying Charles Langdale and Margaret Langdale vagrants from the town of Whitby to the House of Correction at Northallerton

title: Order to pay the constable of Whitby

title: Bill of expenses of the constable of Heworth

title: Private orders [from the Easter Sessions 1833]

title: Report of the Visiting Justices of the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Report of the Visiting Justices of the House of Correction at Northallerton relating to the health, behaviour and numbers of the prisoners, the discontinuation of an allowance of cheese to the prisoners which had been granted during the prevalence of cholera, the earnings of the mill, the cost of victuals, the audit of the Bridgemaster's annual accounts, tradesmen's bills, a proposed reduction in wages because of the low price of corn, the specification of the new bridge at Whitby, the permission for magistrates to pass through the garden of the Register Office, to improve communication between the inn and the Court House, and a proposed alteration of the interior of the Court to provide better accommodation for magistrates, counsel, solicitors and suitors; with a list of the accounts audited by the Visiting Justices

title: Bill of expenses of the constable of Whitby

title: Summary conviction: John Harland
description: Summary conviction of John Harland for trespassing in the daytime in pursuit of game on a close of land in the possession and occupation of James Hindson. Offence committed at the township of Lythe on 22 December 1860. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: John Shaw
description: Summary conviction of John Shaw for being drunk and riotous, fighting in Baxtergate. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 26 December 1860. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: John Carrow

title: Summary conviction: John Green

title: Summary conviction: Mark Noble of Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Peter Wood of Whitby

title: Summary conviction: William Warters

title: Settlement examination: George Miller
description: Settlement examination of George Miller.  For some years until about five or six weeks ago, he gained a livelihood by travelling with a fish cart, carrying cockles from the township of Eston, where he lived, to various towns in the West Riding and elsewhere.  About five or six weeks ago he lost his horse at Whitby, and applied to a schoolmaster at Whitby, whose name he cannot remember, to write him a petition which he got signed by the minister, churchwardens and overseers of the poor of Eston.  He went from Eston to Whitby and other places begging with that petition, and when it was worn to pieces, he got a fresh petition written by Ephraim Jowsey of Loftus yeoman, who copied it from the old one and signed or copied the names of the minister, churchwardens, and overseers of the poor.  He went begging with this petition for about a week, when it was taken from him by a gentleman at East Harlsey, from whom he was asking relief.  He has since been told that this gentleman was Mr Hugill.  He then got a fresh petition copied out from the old one by John Cuthbert of Eston, and continued begging until the present time.  About 30 years ago, he was hired for a year by Martin White of Kirk Merrington in county Durham.  He served him for a year and since then has done nothing to gain a settlement elsewhere

title: Settlement examination: George Brown
description: Settlement examination of George Brown.  He was born at Sunderland in county Durham, and his mother Mary Brown, who is now in a poor house in York, sent him to Hull about two months ago to go to sea on a trial. He was on a vessel called the "Elizabeth and Mary", belonging to James Thompson of Hull.  It went to Sunderland and loaded coals, and then sailed to Holland about a month ago.  After being at sea for some time, it was driven by contrary winds to Leith Roads, where it sprung a leak and took on so much water that the crew took to their boat and landed at Leith.  Brown walked on foot from Leith to Sunderland and then got a passage to Whitby in a lime boat, where he arrived on Thursday or Friday last.  He met his sister in a lodging house, and on the next day they both went to Robin Hood's Bay, and then to Scarborough, and from there to East Ayton.  He begged at every country town and odd house that he passed

title: Settlement examination: Vollantina Brown
description: Settlement examination of Vollantina Brown.  She was born at Liverpool and her brother George Brown, who is now travelling with her, was born at Newcastle upon Tyne.  She lived with her father and mother at Sunderland until about two years ago when her father died.  Afterwards she went to Leeds and there got a pass to Sunderland to look for her settlement.  She stayed at Sunderland for three weeks, but never asked about her settlement.  She travelled from Sunderland to Whitby, and bought mint water and sold it in her travels.  She arrived at Whitby last Saturday week, and went to a lodging house where she met her brother George Brown, who had been there two or three days.  They both left Whitby on Friday last and got to Robin Hood's Bay on the same night.  From there, they went to Scarborough on Saturday last, and were going to York when they were taken up for begging at an odd house in East Ayton

title: Motion to discharge James Leng from the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: Paper to move at the Michaelmas Sessions 1816 for the discharge of James Leng from custody.  Leng had absconded about three years ago from the township of Hutton Bushell, leaving his wife and two children chargeable to the township.  Last July, he was apprehended at Scarborough by William Otterburn, constable and overseer of the poor of Hutton Bushell, and committed on 18 July to the House of Correction.  Otterburn told William Leng, the prisoner's father, that if he paid the £20 incurred for the support of James' wife and family in his absence, then he would procure his release.  William Leng went to Whitby where he had been working for some time to get the £20, but when he got back to Hutton Bushell, he found that Otterburn had already taken his son to the House of Correction.  William Leng paid Otterburn the money on the understanding that it would be returned if James Leng's release could not be obtained

title: Request for mercy for Thomas Morgan
description: Letter from Captain John Hassall at Sunderland to Mr Shepherd at Northallerton Gaol.  He has heard with regret that Thomas Morgan is now a prisoner in Northallerton Gaol.  He served his full term of seven years with Hassall faithfully and honestly and Hassall had no cause for complaint.  Morgan served four years in the "John and Jane" out of Whitby, which was lost, and finished his time out of Sunderland in the "Priscilla"Hassall hopes that Morgan's previous good conduct, his young age, and it being his first offence, will have some weight in the scales of mercy in his favour

title: Order to convey Peter Harry, a vagrant

With examination dated 17 April 1792 of Peter Harry aged 45 years.  He gained his settlement at Whitby, having served a seven-year apprenticeship to John Stevenson of Whitby mariner; and note dated 20 April 1792 to the constable of St Lawrence in the suburbs of York to convey Harry to Heworth on his way to Whitby. title: Bill of indictment for nuisance in not repairing Whitby Bridge: the inhabitants of the North Riding

title: Letter from relating to the status of Whitby and New Malton

title: Letter relating to service as a juror
description: Letter from William Swales at Whitby to Mr R Smithson attorney at Malton.  He believed himself to be exempt from serving on a jury.  He is over 65 years of age, and very infirm, being so lame that he could not get out of his house when he was summoned.  He also has a freehold estate of about £200 a year, and is a younger Brother of Trinity House, Deptford Strand, London.  If a ship-of-war was off the port of Whitby and he was summoned to go on board as a pilot, he cannot refuse to do so except in a case of illness.  He is too lame to ride to the Sessions.  He hopes for all these reasons to be excused the fine for non-attendance

title: Letter relating to service as a juror
description: Letter from Robert Clark at Whitby to Mr Richard Smithson at Malton.  He had been summoned by the bailiff to attend the last Northallerton Sessions as a juror, but as he has more than £150 per annum, he is not liable to serve

title: Letter relating to service as a juror
description: Letter from Robert Clark at Whitby to Mr Wailes, Clerk of the Peace at Stokesley.  Clark had been fined 40s for not attending the last Northallerton Quarter Sessions as a juror.  He has more than £150 per annum and was therefore not liable to be returned as a juror.  He is also verging towards 70 years of age, and is far from being quick of hearing

title: Letter relating to a penalty for refusing to receive Peter Hary, a vagabond

The order to levy £20 was made at the Quarter Sessions held on 12 July 1792.  The chief constable is to pay half of the £20 to the Lord Mayor of York, the first informer, and half to the Treasurer of the North Riding. With letter from Thomas Ewbank to William Wailes esquire at Northallerton relating to the order.  The £20 was going to be paid by Wilkinson's attorney, without the need for the chief constable to make any distress for it.  Also includes a note relating to the case of Gray against Simpkin

Jane, Mary and Esther have not gained a settlement in their own right.  The removal was suspended as the paupers were unable to travel through infirmity- paper to move at the Easter Sessions in April 1835 for the appeal against the removal order to be respited until the next Sessions- paper dated 27 June 1835 relating to the removal of Mary Partington and her children.  Mary's maiden name was Mary Tose.  She married John Partington 20 years ago and had six children all born in the township of Whitby.  Thomas, the youngest, was born after 14 August 1834.  When John Partington married, he already had a wife.  Before her marriage, Mary Tose's settlement was in the township of Egton and she has not gained a settlement elsewhere.  The order of removal will be confirmed only for Mary Tose alias Partington and baby Thomas, and quashed for the other five children, who were born illegitimately in Whitby before 14 August 1834 and therefore belong there [2 copies[DS1]]- order from the Quarter Sessions held on 29 June 1835 confirming the removal of Mary Toes or Partington and her youngest child Thomas, but quashing the removal of the other five children, all born illegitimately in the township of Whitby before 14 August 1834 [Two copies]

title: Papers for an appeal relating to the settlement of Joseph [William] Toes
description: Papers relating to an appeal between the overseers and churchwardens of Egton (appellants) and the overseers and churchwardens of Whitby (respondents) relating to the settlement of Joseph [William] Toes, including:- oath dated 14 April 1817 of Robert Wilson of Whitby gentleman in the case between the overseers and churchwardens of Egton (appellants) and the overseers and churchwardens of Whitby (respondents).  William [sic] Toes the pauper in the appeal is a material witness, but he has absconded.  All efforts have been made to find him- oath dated 15 April 1817 of Robert Wilson of Whitby gentleman in the case between the overseers and churchwardens of Egton (appellants) and the overseers and churchwardens of Whitby (respondents).  Despite enquiries having been made, the indenture of apprenticeship made between Thomas Hunter and Joseph Toes dated 1806 has only just been found.  Wilson was not aware until this morning that John Bell is a witness to the indenture.  John Bell will be a material witness for the appellants, if the court were prepared to await his arrival- undated statement that an attempt will be made to prove a settlement in Whitby or Ruswarp in the first winter of an apprenticeship, before the apprentice went to sea.  The indenture is dated December 1806.  The apprentice did not go to sea until the spring of 1807, and he went where he pleased in the course of that winter and worked for himself as a blacksmith,  He was sometimes at Egton, sometimes Lythe and sometimes Whitby, but not in the service of his master and not provided for by him, and therefore could not gain a settlement anywhere.  A woman has been brought to prove a lodging in Whitby or Ruswarp, but why have they not brought Mr Hunter, who could say that he provided for Toes

title: Examination of Thomas Cholmley, a rogue and vagabond
description: Examination of Thomas Cholmley.  He was born at Hutton near Kendal in Westmorland and when he was about 13 years old, he was apprenticed by indenture to Thomas Harper, then a breeches maker and glover at Lambeth in Surrey.  He served three years at Lambeth and then left by agreement with his master.  He went to sea with Captain Thomas Baddison to the East Indies, and continued as a seaman with different masters and on different voyages until about five or six years ago, when he "got a misfortune" that made him unfit to continue to be a sailor.  Since then he has gone round the country selling corks, blue and other articles but without having a hawker's licence.  About a week ago, when he had disposed of almost all of his goods at Scarborough, he set off for Kendal.  He came through Whitby to Guisborough on Thursday night last, where he lodged.  On the Friday morning he went back to Skelton in order to get a pass from John Wharton esquire of Skelton Castle, but was apprehended as a rogue and vagabond

title: Examination of Thomas Howlston
description: Examination of Thomas Howlston.  He was born at Kirkdale about two miles from Liverpool, and was apprenticed to Peter Williamson of Liverpool staymaker for seven years.  He served about three years and has lived at Liverpool until about a year and a half ago, when he went to Edinburgh in Scotland.  He was taken ill there, and was ill for about ten months, and then travelled around the country seeking work.  He left Berwick about two months ago, and came through Darlington, Yarm, Stokesley, Guisborough, Whitby and Scarborough, and was intending to go to Liverpool when he was apprehended yesterday for begging in Hutton Bushell

title: Settlement examination of Luke Flynn
description: Settlement examination of Luke Flynn a rogue and vagabond.  He was born at Wicklow in Ireland and bound apprentice to Captain Hopkin Harris of Dublin to serve as a seaman for seven years.  He served about five years of his apprenticeship, and in 1745 he was impressed on board the "Royal Sovereign" ship-of-war at the Nore.  Afterwards he served on the "Raven" a sloop-of-war, and has since served on different ships-of-war and in the Merchant Service.  He came from Plymouth with his wife Ann about three months ago, and they were travelling to Whitby when they asked for relief at Pickering

title: Letters from John Calvert at Whitby relating to his position as bailiff
description: Letters from John Calvert at Whitby relating to his position as bailiff, including:- letter dated 27 June 1791 from John Calvert at Whitby to Mr Joseph Burke attorney at law at Malton.  On 21 May [1791] Calvert was deputed as bailiff by the executors of the late Nathannil [sic] Cholmley esquire, to replace Zachariah Knaggs.  He asks for the names of those who are to be jurors at the next Quarter Sessions, so that he can pass on necessary information- letter dated 30 June 1791 from John Calvert at Whitby to Mr Richard Smithson deputy sheriff at Malton.  He apologises for not replying by return as he got the letter at 12 o'clock and the post goes out at 1 o'clock.  He had to go two miles to Zacharias Knaggs to ask for the lists of jurors, but got nothing but abuse and bad language.  Knaggs came to town with him and promised to call in the evening, but he went home "much ellevated [sic] in liquor".  His reason for not giving Calvert the lists was to favour one person, but Calvert leaves it to Smithson to judge who that person might be- letter dated 2 July 1791 from John Calvert at Whitby to Mr Richard Smithson deputy sheriff at Malton.  He has received Smithson's warrant, and Zacheriah [sic] Knaggs delivered up his warrant last evening, when Mr Brown the chief constable went to him and persuaded him to do so.  Calvert executed the process on John Mahorn and his wife, and Bowes is at Greenland and his wife cannot be found.  Calvert will summon the jurors listed in the warrant

title: Bill of expenses and order to pay the constable of Fylingdales
description: Order dated 3 July 1817 to the High Constable of Whitby Strand to pay a reward to John Smallwood constable of Fylingdales blacksmith for apprehending John Place, found begging in Fylingdales, and for bringing him before the Justices.  Annotated with a receipt for 10s given to Smallwood by Thomas Galilee Dale. Bill of expenses dated 3 July 1817 of John Smallwood constable of Fylingdales for a warrant to commit John Place for begging in Fylingdales, and for taking him to Northallerton.  Smallwood swore to the truth of his account on 12 July 1817[The order and bill are attached together]

title: Bill of expenses of the constable of Whitby
description: Bill of expenses of John Morley of Whitby relating to:- apprehending Martha Stockton for felony on 28 April 1817, and taking her from Whitby to York Castle on 1 May 1817- taking Ann Stockton from Whitby to York Castle on 26 May 1817- "long and special" examinations of Joseph Trott, William Hartley and John Morley, prior to taking William Mead and Robert Mead to York Castle on 26 May 1817 for cutting and maiming. Endorsed "Whitby constable"

title: Bill of expenses and order to pay the constable of Whitby
description: Bill of expenses of the constable of Whitby for a warrant to commit John Cambel for begging in Whitby, and for taking him to Northallerton.  William Dobson special constable swore to the truth of this account. Order to the High Constable of Whitby Strand to pay a reward to Thomas Nettleship [William Dobson deleted] for apprehending John Cambel and bringing him before the Justices.  Endorsed with a receipt for 10s paid to Nettleship on 12 July by Mr T.G. Dale[The bill and order are attached together]

title: Certificate for returns of corn and oatmeal: Whitby

title: Bill of expenses for the conveyance of wounded soldiers and their baggage

title: Bill of expenses of Alfred Simpson

title: Calendar of prisoners in the House of Correction at Northallerton
description: A calendar of prisoners in the House of Correction at Northallerton who are to be tried at the Sessions to be held at Northallerton on Tuesday 14 October 1817; and also those still confined, or who have been discharged at or since the last Quarter Sessions.  Includes:Felony- William Binks aged 29 years, John Mines aged 24 years, and Matthew West aged 19 years; committed on 24 July 1817 for having escaped from the House of Correction- Elizabeth Exley aged 19 years, late of New Malton; committed on 7 August 1817 for stealing and pawning a printed cotton shawl, the property of Hannah Mason of New Malton- William Stephenson aged 15 years, late of Whitby; committed on 26 September 1817 for stealing a basket and pots.  He was charged on the oath of Mary Bettany wife of James Bettany of Knottingley in the West Riding, whose property it was- George Ling aged 19 years and Elizabeth Ling aged 16 years; committed on 9 October 1817 for stealing a cotton gown and a cotton bedgown, the property of Barbara York of Great Ayton singlewoman. Misdemeanours- Frances Thornton aged 18 years, wife of Mark Thornton, late of Northallerton; convicted and committed on 30 July 1817 as a vagrant, having been found begging in the township of Northallerton- Thomas Lee aged 15 years, late of Pickering; convicted and committed on 28 July 1817 as a vagrant- Simon Austen aged 25 years, late of Orion in Westmorland; committed on 1 August 1817 for refusing to find sureties to indemnify the township of High Abbotside for the maintenance of the bastard child of Betty Brown of High Abbotside, and for his appearance at Quarter Sessions- John Dyson aged 18 years, late of Halifax in the West Riding; committed on 14 August 1817 as a vagrant, having been found begging in the township of Guisborough without having a legal settlement there- George Pearson aged 19 years, late of Pickering; committed on 17 August 1817 for disobeying an order for the maintenance of the bastard son of Agnes Watson of Brompton in the wapentake of Pickering Lythe- Thomas McConnell aged 26 years; committed on 27 August 1817 on the oath of George Barker, for wandering in the township of Easingwold and not giving a good account of himself- Elizabeth Down aged 37 years, Thomas Down aged 11 years, Francis Down aged 9 years, and Margaret Down aged 6 years; committed on 27 August 1817 as a vagrant, having been  found begging in the township of Easingwold without having gained a legal settlement there- Joseph Brind aged 24 years, Mary Martin aged 19 years and Mary Robertson aged 25 years; committed on 27 August 1817 as vagrants, having been found begging in the township of Easingwold without having gained a legal settlement there- Ann Barrass aged 28 years and Mary Barrass aged 6 years; committed on 27 August 1817 as vagrants, having been found begging in the township of Easingwold without having gained a legal settlement there- Mary Hudson aged 66 years, Rachael Nicholson aged 59 years and Penelope Nicholson aged 18 years; committed on 27 August 1817 as vagrants, having been found begging in the township of Easingwold without having a legal settlement there.  Mary Hudson had been committed to this prison on one previous occasion- Sarah Reed aged 16 years; committed on 27 August 1817 as a vagrant, having been found begging in the township of Easingwold without having gained a legal settlement there- Mary Steward aged 52 years, John Peroe aged 20 years and Adron Almingham aged 61 years; committed on 27 August 1817 as vagrants, having been found begging in the township of Easingwold without having gained a legal settlement there- John Thomas Motha aged 29 years; convicted and committed on 11 September 1817 as a vagrant, having been found wandering in the township of Easingwold and not giving a good account of himself- James Hutchinson aged 20 years; convicted and committed on 27 September 1817 as a vagrant, having been found wandering in the township of Guisborough with a suspicious discharge from the army- Jane Hardy aged 59 years, Thomas Donn aged 18 years and Jane Donn aged 15 years; committed on 27 September 1817 as vagrants, quarrelling and behaving in a tumultuous manner in the township of Guisborough, without having gained a legal settlement there- William Toas aged 21 years; committed on 6 October 1817 as a vagrant, and for absenting himself from his wife and family leaving them chargeable to the township of Egton. Under sentence of confinement- Ann Owthett aged 20 years; received in the House of Correction on 2 November 1816 for privately stealing goods from a shop.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for one year, after the Prince Regent extended the Royal Mercy to her, she having been convicted at York and had the death sentence passed on her- Mark Towler aged 24 years; received in the House of Correction on 21 March 1817 for grand larceny.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for one year- William Hodgson aged 36 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 April 1817 for felony.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for 12 months- John Howard aged 38 years; received in the House of Correction on 16 May 1817 for stealing a lamb.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for one year, after the Prince Regent extended the Royal Mercy to him, he having been convicted at York and had the death sentence passed on him- Elizabeth Crawford aged 21 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 July 1817 for felony.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for six calendar months hard labour.  Committed to this prison on one previous occasion- Thomas Turner aged 26 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 July 1817 for felony.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for four calendar months hard labour- Charles Landels aged 19 years and Peter Walker aged 16 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 July 1817 for felony.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for four calendar months hard labour- George Willey aged 55 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 July 1817 for assault.  Sentenced to be imprisoned until he find sureties.  Committed to this prison on one previous occasion- Joseph Leng aged 28 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 July 1817 for assault and escape from the constable of New Malton.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for six months.  Committed to this prison on one previous occasion- George Carter aged 59 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 July 1817 for felony.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for three calendar months hard labour- William Taylor aged 30 years, William Hodgson aged 23 years and John Hodgson aged 22 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 July 1817 for breaking open the prison at New Malton.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for three calendar months and to pay a fine of 6d each.  John Hodgson had been confined to this prison on one previous occasion- William Langthorn aged 27 years; received in the House of Correction on 31 July 1817, for disobeying an order of bastardy.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for three months hard labour- William Codling aged 20 years; received in the House of Correction on 22 August 1817, for disobeying an order of bastardy.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for three months hard labour- Ralph Squince aged 25 years; received in the House of Correction on 6 September 1817, for disobeying an order of bastardy.  Sentenced to be imprisoned for three months hard labour. Committed but later discharged:- John Younghusband aged 38 years; received into the House of Correction on 16 July 1816 for felony.  Imprisoned for 12 calendar months- Rebecca Ward aged 28 years; received in the House of Correction on 20 September 1816 for being lewd and disorderly.  Imprisoned for 12 months- Thomas Osleton aged 36 years; received in the House of Correction on 14 January 1817 for assault.  Found the sureties required- Joseph Anderson aged 18 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 April 1817 for felony.  Imprisoned for six months- George Cleghorn aged 34 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 April 1817 for uttering and tendering counterfeit silver tokens.  Imprisoned for six months and found the sureties required- William Bland aged 36 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 April 1817 for felony.  Imprisoned for four months- James Woodhouse aged 48 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 April 1817 for felony.  Imprisoned for six months- William Hedger aged 26 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 April 1817 for bastardy.  Liberated by W. Dent clerk- John Weatherill aged 18 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 April 1817 for felony.  Escaped from the House of Correction on 22 July 1822- William Buckle aged 25 years; received in the House of Correction on 16 April 1817 for felony.  Discharged by the court- John Leng aged 35 years; received in the House of Correction on 23 April 1817 for disobeying an order of bastardy.  Imprisoned for three months- Elizabeth Porter aged 69 years and Mary Porter aged 14 years; received in the House of Correction on 24 April 1817 for vagrancy. Ordered by the court to be passed- Joseph Aveson aged 20 years; received in the House of Correction on 3 June 1817 for assault. Imprisoned for three months- Ann Woodall aged 48 years; received in the House of Correction on 6 June 1817 for assault.  Discharged by the court- Thomas Tatham aged 27 years; received in the House of Correction on 13 June 1817 for trespass.  Imprisoned for two months- John Barker aged 15 years; received in the House of Correction on 20 June 1817 for absenting himself from his apprenticeship.  Discharged by the court- Mary Langthorn aged 25 years; received in the House of Correction on 23 June 1817 for disobeying an order of removal.  Imprisoned for one month- George Ruddock aged 42 years; received in the House of Correction on 30 June 1817 for assault.  Discharged by the court- John Place aged 36 years; received in the House of Correction on 4 July 1817 for vagrancy.  Discharged by the court- James Metcalfe aged 31 years; received in the House of Correction on 12 July 1817 for assault. Ordered by the court to be passed- Elizabeth Sheffield aged 25 years; received in the House of Correction on 15 July 1817 for felony.  Imprisoned for one calendar month- John Mawman aged 29 years; received in the House of Correction on 16 July 1817 for vagrancy.  Imprisoned for one month- John Fawell aged 27 years; received in the House of Correction on 16 July 1817 for disobeying an order of bastardy.  Liberated by R. Blanshard esquire- Henry Nevison aged 31 years; received in the House of Correction on 23 July 1817 for assault.  Liberated by R. Blanshard esquire- John Saville aged 83 years; received in the House of Correction on 24 July 1817 for misbehaviour.  Imprisoned for one month- Isaac Pearson aged 37 years and Thomas Archer aged 47 years; received in the House of Correction on 5 August 1817 for vagrancy.  Imprisoned for seven days and passed- William Collinson aged 28 years and Joseph Smith aged 45 years; received in the House of Correction on 6 August 1817 for misdemeanour.  Liberated on bail by R. Blanshard esquire- Hannah Watson aged 28 years; received in the House of Correction on 8 August 1817 for vagrancy.  Imprisoned for one month- David Edwards aged 24 years; received in the House of Correction on 9 August 1817 for vagrancy.  Imprisoned for seven days and passed- William Fowler aged 19 years; received in the House of Correction on 9 August 1817 for absenting himself from his apprenticeship.  Imprisoned for one calendar month- Simon Hunton aged 53 years; received in the House of Correction on 23 August 1817 for vagrancy. title: Special orders from the Easter Sessions 1836
description: Bundle of papers relating to Special Orders at the Easter Sessions 1836.  Many of the papers are numbered, and the number in square brackets after each entry is that original number.  Includes:- recommendation dated 22 March 1836 of John Chapman of Low Stakesby Hall as a fit person to have his name inserted in the Commission of the Peace for the North Riding [1]- letter dated 7 March 1836 from Richard Moorson at Airy Hill to the Revd John Headlam at Wycliffe.  He forwards the names of John Holt of Cliff House and John Glover Loy of Ewe Cote Hall, both in Whitby Strand, for insertion in the Commission of the Peace, and intends to recommend them to the Bench at the next Sessions [2]- letter dated 4 April 1836 from George Lloyd of Cowesby Manor and William Dent to the chairman of Quarter Sessions.  He asks for the name of the Revd Francis Henson of South Kilvington to be inserted in the Commission of the Peace [3]- letter dated 4 April 1836 from H. Croft at Stillington to the chairman of Quarter Sessions at Northallerton.  Indisposition prevents him from attending the Sessions, where he would have proposed Francis Cholmley esquire of Brandsby as a suitable person to be a magistrate in the division of Bulmer.  Mr Stapleton of Myton will second the proposal [4]- report dated 4 April 1836 of the Visiting Justices of the House of Correction relating to discipline, adherence to regulations, the rule of silence, the number of prisoners, and accounts [5]- undated draft order that William Lawson esquire of Brough should be appointed a Visiting Justice in place of R.W. Pierce esquire, who has resigned [6]- undated draft order that the thanks of the Court be given to the Finance Committee and they be asked to continue until the next Sessions.  Joshua S. Crompton esquire is to be added to the Finance Committee.  The report of the Visiting Justices is to be received, and they are to be asked to continue.  William Lawson esquire of Brough Hall is to be appointed as a Visiting Justice in place of Mr Peirce [sic] who has resigned [7]- undated note that all prisoners, both male and female, should be placed under the Silence System [8]- undated order for the Visiting Justices to apply to the magistrates of the city and Ainsty of York and the boroughs of Richmond and Scarborough for payment of their share of the expenses incurred in the registration of voters [9]- undated note that Mr Yeoman had explained his reasons preventing his attendance at the General Gaol Sessions in the last Assize week to support a notice for a new apportionment of the county rate-  The Clerk of the Peace is to repeat the notice for the next Assizes [10]- motion paper dated 4 April 1836 from W Mauleverer esquire for all magistrates to attend on the Friday before every Sessions to audit the current accounts of the Riding for the preceding Quarter, as is the practice in the West Riding [11]- undated list of receipts and disbursements for the Christmas Sessions 1836- notes dated 4 April 1836 on bridges in need of repair, including Tocketts Bridge, Thornton Bridge, Yarm Bridge, Sandbeck Bridge and Wath Bridge- notice dated 4 April 1836 of a motion for the next Quarter Sessions to be submitted by William Mauleverer esquire, that all bills of costs for prosecutions or any other expenses should not be discharged until the Sessions after that in which they were incurred, so that they may be examined and sanctioned by the Finance Committee before payment- undated order for the Bridge Master to enter into contracts for the repair of roads and bridges with the Trustees of the Turnpike Roads at a lower rate than the present ones.  The plea of not guilty relating to the presentment of Bishopdale Bridge is to be withdrawn, and a special plea filed for the constabulary of Thoralby to pay pro rata for the repair of the bridge.  The constabulary had been relieved of the expense of repairing a foot bridge after the present bridge was built- undated order that the Clerk of the Peace move the Court at the next Sessions to discharge the presentment of York Castle for an insufficiency of classification.  This order is endorsed "Special Orders"

title: Calendar of prisoners at the House of Correction at Thirsk
description: A calendar of prisoners committed to the House of Correction at Thirsk, including for what, when, and by whom committed. Committed on 3 May 1788- John Harpur for wandering in the township of Helmsley Blackamoor without having a legal settlement there.  Committed on 3 May 1788- John Williamson and George Phillips for begging in the township of Stokesley without having a legal settlement there.  Committed on 21 May 1788- Ann Campion, charged on the oath of Mary Yeoman at Barnby with assaulting and threatening her.  Committed on 24 May 1788- William Wilkinson otherwise Scarr, charged on suspicion of stealing a linen web value 30s, the property of William Allen and taken from the bleach yard of John Flounders of Crathorne. Committed 10 June 1788- Grace wife of John Bradley of Whitby, charged on the oath of Elizabeth Bradley of Whitby with stealing her cotton gown and petticoat.  Committed on 20 June 1788- Robert Dalton, charged on the oath of Daniel Ling of Whitby for assaulting and beating him on 21 June 1788.  Committed on 24 June 1788- Hannah Thackery for begging in the parish of Pickering, without having a legal settlement there.  Committed on 25 June 1788- William Wood, charged with assaulting and beating Thomas Blenkey of Appleton Wiske while he (Blenkey) was deputy to John Mawer constable of Appleton Wiske. Committed on 27 June 1788- a man wandering in the parish of Whitby, and refusing to give any account of himself, pretending to be dumb. Committed on 9 July 1788. title: Warrant to levy a fine on the inhabitants of Lockton
description: Warrant for the constables of Pickering and West Ayton to raise £23 9s 2d to pay compensation to Richard Hill by distraining the goods and chattels of the acting Inclosure Commissioners for Lockton. At the Quarter Sessions held on 17 April 1787, it was reported that at the previous Quarter Sessions held at Easingwold on 9 January 1787, Richard Hill, on behalf of himself and the other inhabitants of Thornton and Farmanby, had appealed against the stopping-up and diverting by the Inclosure Commissioners of a road in the parish of Lockton leading from Thornton and Farmanby to Whitby.  Hearing of the appeal was respited to the next Quarter Sessions, and three Justices were requested to visit the road and report back. According to their report, the new road was longer and less commodious to the public than the old road, and the old road was ordered to be re-opened, and compensation paid to Richard Hill for his expenses in the appeal. At the Quarter Sessions on 15 January 1788 it was found that the John Foord and Robert King, acting Commissioners, had not yet paid the compensation. Annotated with a receipt dated 7 April 1788 for money for compensation and cost, given to John Bell attorney for Richard Hill esquire by Matthew Rowntree constable of Pickering

Levinson had been apprehended for begging in the township of Whitby

description: Recognizance made by Isabella Fewster of Whitby widow for her appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to prefer a bill of indictment against William Batty for assaulting her

title: Bill of indictment for felony: William Batey or Batty of the House of Correction at Thirsk
description: Bill of indictment of William Batey otherwise William Batty late of the House of Correction at Thirsk mariner for stealing one man's hat value 6d, the property of Isabel Fewster. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 24 September 1788. Endorsed with name of witness and "a true bill"

title: Calendar of prisoners at the House of Correction at Thirsk
description: A calendar of prisoners committed to the House of Correction at Thirsk, giving for what, when and by whom committed- William Carradine, indicted for assaulting Thomas Atkinson of Pickering.  Ordered at the Quarter Sessions held at Stokesley to be imprisoned in the House of Correction until the next Sessions, unless he can find sureties for his appearance and for trying his traverse- John Pybus, indicted for a felony.  Ordered at the Quarter Sessions held by adjournment at Thirsk to be imprisoned in the House of Correction at Thirsk until the next Sessions- Catherine Webdale, Mary her daughter and Thomas her son, vagrants found begging in the township of Kirby Moorside without having a legal settlement there, and committed on 19 July 1788- Thomas Gibson, committed on 28 July 1788 for refusing to find sureties for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions, and for keeping the peace in the meantime especially towards Henry Atley of Whitby- James Lamb, apprehended in the township of Appleton Wiske and convicted as a vagrant.  Committed on 11 August 1788- Susanna Stephens, a vagrant found begging in the township of Whitby without having a legal settlement there.  On 31 May 1788 she gave birth to a daughter at Whitby, and has become chargeable to the township of Whitby.  Committed on 14 August 1788- Peter Kennedy, a vagrant found lodging in outhouses in the township of Whitby, without giving a good account of himself.  Committed on 20 August 1788- Michael Leadham, a vagrant found begging in the township of Whitby, without giving a good account of himself.  Committed on 20 August 1788- Mary wife of Simon Leadham, a vagrant pretending to be deaf and dumb, and telling fortunes in the township of Whitby.  Committed on 20 August 1788- Mary Wrigglesworth, committed on 22 August 1788 for refusing to find sureties for her appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to answer a bill of indictment brought against her by Margaret Raper of Northallerton for an assault- William Taylor, Elizabeth his wife, and their children Ann and William, vagrants, found begging in the township of Whitby and using subtle craft to deceive and impose on people.  William Taylor refused to give a good account of himself.  Committed on 3 September 1788- Robert Dawson, committed on 14 September 1788 charged with stealing part of a sheaf of oats value 2d, the property of William Smith of South Otterington- Mary wife of Thomas Marley late of Great Ayton, committed on 19 September 1788 charged on suspicion of felony in stealing two yards of linen cloth from the house of Ann Taylorson of the township of Great Ayton widow- William Batty, committed on 26 September 1788, charged on the oath of Isabella Fewster of Whitby who is afraid that Batty will beat or kill her- Hannah Hobb, committed on 27 September 1788 and charged with stealing a pair of women's shoes from the house of Thomas Fairfoot- John Bains, committed on 31 May 1788 charged on the oath of Mary Whitehawk of the township of Aldwark with having made her pregnant, and for want of sureties for his appearance- Allan Gray, committed on 16 September 1788 charged on the oath of Enoch Craike of Wath with having left his apprenticeship on 10 May 1785 until the present time.  To be imprisoned in the House of Correction at Thirsk for three months- William Hopwood, to remain in the House of Correction at Thirsk- Augustine Metcalf, to remain in the House of Correction at Thirsk- William Fewler, committed on 2 October 1788 charged on suspicion of felony in stealing two panniers of herrings value 11s, the property of Margaret Ripley of Redcar- Edward Taylor, committed on 4 October 1788 on the oath of Mary Hardwith of Pickering, with having made her pregnant, and for want of sureties for his appearance

title: Precept, call roll and lists of jurors for the Michaelmas Quarter Sessions 1788

title: Bill of expenses for precepts: Whitby Strand division
description: Bill of expenses of William Wilkinson the younger late high constable of the division of Whitby Strand for precepts issued between the Easter Sessions 1857 and the Michaelmas Sessions 1857 relating to transferring ale licences, the highway appeal day, jury lists, the general annual licensing day, and for stamping weights and measures

title: Order to pay for examining weights and measures in Whitby Strand division
description: Order to the Treasurer of the North Riding to pay the representatives of William Wilkinson and his assistant for eight days spent examining weights, measures and balances in the division of Whitby Strand between July and October 1857

title: Bill of expenses of the returning officer for Whitby
description: Bill of the returning officer for the borough of Whitby for his expenses between June and October 1856, with the proportion of the total to be paid by each of the three townships of Whitby. With a bill from Horne and Son, printing, bookselling etc establishment in Whitby, for expenses incurred by Mr Gray the returning officer for the borough of Whitby between July and October, including printing the register of voters

title: Report of the Police Committee
description: Report to the Michaelmas Quarter Sessions of the Police Committee, relating to a table of fees and allowances, a proposed lock-up house at Thirsk, the need for printed forms for the returns of fines and fees, the need for the appointment of officers to inspect weights and measures in Whitby and Hallikeld divisions, and a scheme for the division of the constabulary into police districts

title: Motion paper relating to the inspection of weights and measures
description: Paper to move that the superintendent of constabulary at Whitby should also be appointed as Inspector of Weights and Measures for that division, and the inspector at Bedale should be appointed to inspect weights and measures for Hallikeld division

title: Notice relating to cleaning the rooms used for Petty Sessions at Whitby Strand
description: Notice given to the Clerk of the Peace by three Justices for the Petty Sessional division of Whitby Strand that they intend to apply at the next Quarter Sessions for an order to be made to pay for cleaning the rooms used for Petty Sessions. Annotated "Received 27 July 1857"

title: Papers relating to the removal of Ann Brown from Whitby to Monkwearmouth in county Durham
description: Papers relating to the removal of Ann Brown from Whitby to Monkwearmouth in county Durham, including:- copy order dated 18 August 1857 for the removal of Ann Brown from the township of Whitby to the township of Monkwearmouth in county Durham- notice dated 30 September 1857 given by the overseers of the poor of the township of Monkwearmouth in county Durham, to the overseers of the poor of the township of Whitby.  They intend to appeal at the next Quarter Sessions against the removal order of 18 August 1857, and give their grounds for the appeal.  With copy- receipt for a registered letter dated 1 October 1857 and addressed to the overseers of the poor of the township of Whitby- notice dated 15 October 1857 from the churchwardens and overseers of the poor of the township of Whitby to the churchwardens and  overseers of the poor of the township of Monkwearmouth in county Durham abandoning the removal order

title: Summary conviction: Richard Knaggs of Ellerby
description: Summary conviction of Richard Knaggs of the township of Ellerby labourer for trespassing in the daytime in search and pursuit of game on land in the possession and occupation of William Hodgson; on the information of Henry William Siggs of the township of Lythe gamekeeper. Offence committed at the township of Ellerby at 3 p.m. on 20 June 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Henry Webster of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of Henry Webster of the township of Whitby labourer for assaulting and resisting Hugh MacGregor in the execution of his office; on the oath of the said Hugh MacGregor of the township of Ruswarp superintendent of police and constable. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 4 July 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Henry Webster of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of Henry Webster of the township of Whitby labourer for assaulting and resisting George Jackson in the execution of his office; on the oath of the said George Jackson of the township of Whitby police constable. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 4 July 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Thomas Walker
description: Summary conviction of Thomas Walker apprentice by an indenture dated 11 May 1857 to John Milburn of the township of Ruswarp shipowner, for absconding from his master's service. Offence committed on 11 May 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Ralph Nunn of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of Ralph Nunn of the township of Whitby ship carpenter for assaulting John Mason of the township of Whitby butcher; on the oath of the said John Mason and another. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 19 July 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: George Wilson of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of George Wilson of the township of Whitby ship carpenter for assaulting John Mason of the township of Whitby butcher; on the oath of the said John Mason and others. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 19 July 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Thomas Jackson
description: Summary conviction of Thomas Jackson a reputed thief, for frequenting Whitby harbour for the purpose of committing felony. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 24 July 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Esther Anthony of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of Esther Anthony wife of Joyce Anthony of the township of Whitby mariner for using obscene and indecent language in Church Street; on the oath of Robert Nickson of the township of Whitby police constable. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 26 July 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: James Farrah of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of James Farrah of the township of Whitby labourer for using obscene and indecent language in Church Street; on the oath of Robert Nickson of the township of Whitby police constable. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 26 July 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Mary Ashton
description: Summary conviction of Mary Ashton for trading as a petty chapman without being licensed. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 5 August 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Thomas Jackson
description: Summary conviction of Thomas Jackson a suspected person and reputed thief for frequenting the river Esk with intent to commit felony. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 11 September 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Mark Herbert of Fylingdales
description: Summary conviction of Mark Herbert of the township of Fylingdales farmer for being drunk; on the oath of George Bushell of the township of Fylingdales police constable. Offence committed at the township of Fylingdales on 11 September 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: John Furniss late of Hartlepool in county Durham
description: Summary conviction of John Furniss late of the parish of Hartlepool in county Durham fisherman for wilfully damaging two herring nets value £5, the property of Robert Harrison; on the oath of the said Robert Harrison of the parish of Durham [sic] fisherman. Offence committed at the parish of Whitby on 28 September 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: James Haley late of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of James Haley late of the township of Whitby labourer for assaulting and resisting Hugh McGregor in the execution of his office; on the oath of the said Hugh McGregor of the township of Ruswarp superintendent of police and constable for the North Riding. Offence committed at the township of Whitby on 22 September 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Richard Hill the younger of Newholm cum Dunsley
description: Summary conviction of Richard Hill the younger of the township of Newholm cum Dunsley labourer for killing a hare; on the information of Henry William Siggs of the township of Lythe gamekeeper and others. Offence committed at the township of Lythe on Sunday 13 September 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Joseph Breckon of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of Joseph Breckon of the township of Whitby stonemason for killing a hare; on the information of Henry William Siggs of the township of Lythe gamekeeper and others. Offence committed at the township of Lythe on Sunday 13 September 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Robert Goodwill of Whitby
description: Summary conviction of Robert Goodwill of the township of Whitby stonemason for using a gun to kill game; on the information of Henry William Siggs of the township of Lythe gamekeeper and others. Offence committed at the township of Lythe on Sunday 13 September 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: Isaac Patton late of Hinderwell
description: Summary conviction of Isaac Patton late of the township of Hinderwell labourer for killing three hares at night on Runswick Lane. Offence committed at the township of Mickleby on 3 October 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: John Craven late of Hinderwell
description: Summary conviction of John Craven late of the township of Hinderwell labourer for killing three hares at night on Runswick Lane. Offence committed at the township of Mickleby on 3 October 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Summary conviction: John Calvert late of Hinderwell
description: Summary conviction of John Calvert late of the township of Hinderwell for killing three hares at night on Runswick Lane. Offence committed at the township of Mickleby on 3 October 1857. Case heard at Whitby

title: Monthly return of fines: Whitby Strand division
description: Monthly return to the Justices for the Petty Sessional division of Whitby Strand of fines received by the clerk of the Court between 1 July 1857 and 31 July 1857.  Includes names of parties convicted, date of conviction, offence, costs and fines paid, and names of convicting magistrates

title: Monthly return of fines: Whitby Strand division
description: Monthly return to the Justices for the Petty Sessional division of Whitby Strand of fines received by the clerk of the Court between 1 August 1857 and 31 August 1857.  Includes names of parties convicted, date of conviction, offence, costs and fines paid, and names of convicting magistrates

title: Monthly return of fines: Whitby Strand division
description: Monthly return to the Justices for the Petty Sessional division of Whitby Strand of fines received by the clerk of the Court between 1 September 1857 and 30 September 1857.  Includes names of parties convicted, date of conviction, offence, costs and fines paid, punishment when fine not paid and reason for non-payment, and names of convicting magistrates

title: Evidence relating to the case against George Corner late of Whitby
description: Information and complaint dated 8 September 1857 of Benjamin Waller of the parish of Lythe master mariner against George Corner late of the parish of Whitby mariner. Depositions dated 10 September 1857 of Benjamin Waller of the parish of Lythe master mariner, William Reid mariner and Samuel Thompson police constable, both of Whitby , and John Clarkson of the parish of Lythe police constable, witnesses in the case against George Corner. Statement dated 10 September 1857 of George Corner, the accused. With separate cover sheet

title: Evidence relating to the case against Thomas Gill of Whitby
description: Depositions of Robert Burt Hall civil engineer and John Davies miner, both of Danby, witnesses in the case against Thomas Gill of Whitby labourer. Statement of Thomas Gill, the accused

title: Recognizances in the case against George Corner late of Whitby
description: Recognizance made by Benjamin Waller of the parish of Lythe master mariner for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to prefer a bill of indictment against George Corner late of the township of Whitby for stealing a telescope, a blue cloth jacket, two pairs of fustian trousers, two pairs of flannel drawers, a sleeved waistcoat, and a flannel shirt from a ship called the "Thomas" in Whitby harbour. Recognizance made by Samuel Thompson of the township of Whitby police constable for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to give evidence in the case against George Corner. Recognizance made by John Clarkson of the township of Lythe police constable for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to give evidence in the case against George Corner. With separate cover sheet

title: Recognizances in the case against Thomas Gill of Whitby
description: Recognizance made by Robert Burt Hall of Danby civil engineer for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to prefer a bill of indictment against Thomas Gill of Whitby labourer for causing him grievous bodily harm. Recognizance made by John Davies of Danby miner for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to give evidence in the case against Thomas Gill. Recognizance made by Thomas Gill of Whitby labourer, and William Plews miller and Thomas Ruddock farmer, both of Castleton, for the appearance of Gill at the next Quarter Sessions to answer the case against him

title: Recognizances in the case against Nathan Wilson late of Kirby Misperton
description: Recognizance made by William Wilson of Hamer in the parish of Middleton innkeeper for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to prefer a bill of indictment against Nathan Wilson late of Kirby Misperton labourer for stealing a promissory note for £5 called a Whitby Old Bank note and a sovereign from him. Recognizance made by Thomas Gibson of Wrelton police constable for his appearance at the next Quarter Sessions to give evidence in the case against Nathan Wilson. With separate cover sheet

title: Abstract of coroner's inquests for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand
description: An abstract of inquisitions taken by John Hancock gentleman, coroner for the liberty of Whitby and Whitby Strand, and given in at the Lent Assizes 1782 held at the Castle of York. Ten inquests are listed:- Richard Johnson.  Inquest held at Whitby on 12 September 1781.  Verdict: drowned- James Day.  Inquest held at Ruswarp on 12 September 1781.  Verdict: accident- Richard Sedman.  Inquest held at Fylingdales on 12 October 1781.  Verdict: died of a fit- William Nichols.  Inquest held at Ruswarp on 24 October 1781.  Verdict: drowned- William Tillart.  Inquest held at Whitby on 17 November 1781.  Verdict: accident- Ann Coulthirst.  Inquest held at Fylingdales on 28 November 1781.  Verdict: died of a fit- Archibald Armstrong.  Inquest held at Fylingdales on 6 February 1782.  Verdict: visitation of almighty God- Robert Johnson.  Inquest held at Whitby on 21 February 1782.  Verdict: accident- John Peak.  Inquest held at Whitby on 21 February 1782.  Verdict: accident- George Elliot.  Inquest held at Newholm on 9 March 1782.  Verdict: found dead

description: Bill dated 2 March 1782 of money owed by William Atley constable of the township of Whitby to Thomas Seamer for conveying Sarah Scott to the Castle of York.  Bill allowed on 9 March 1782

title: Bill of expenses of the constable of Ugthorpe
description: Bill of expenses of the constable of Ugthorpe for conveying Thomas Reighton to York Castle for breaking into the dwelling house of William Ripley at Ugthorpe and stealing a silver watch. Endorsed "Constable of Whitby"

title: Bill of expenses of the constable of Whitby
description: Bill of expenses dated 24 December 1787 of Thomas Anderson constable of Whitby for conveying Ann Wriglesworth singlewoman from Whitby to the House of Correction at Thirsk for felony.  Bill allowed on 12 January

title: Bill of expenses of the constable of Whitby
description: Bill of expenses dated 26 December 1787 of Thomas Anderson constable of Whitby for conveying George Child mariner from Whitby to the House of Correction at Thirsk for felony.  Bill allowed on 12 January

title: Bill of expenses of the constable of Whitby
description: Bill of expenses dated 9 January 1788 of Thomas Anderson constable of Whitby for conveying Robert Good carpenter from Whitby to York Castle for felony.  Bill allowed on 12 January

description: Order to the Treasurer for the North Riding to pay John Galloway constable of the township of Reeth for conveying James Nichalson a parish apprentice bound to the sea service to the port of Whitby, where Charles Noddings his master belongs

title: Orders to pay the constable of Bowes
description: Undated summary of expenses to be paid to William Hobson constable of Bowes for conveying vagrants. Order dated 22 December 1787- conveying Charles Brawbins, a vagrant, from the township of Bowes to Barnard Castle in county Durham.
